Legal record (#67) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 22v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 27 [El]ul 5324 CE (1564 CE). Debt settlement and partnership dissolution between Yiṣḥaq b. David al-Kohen, aka בעלם(?) (ʿIlm?), and Yosef b. Ṣedaqa, aka Naqqash, in connection with a shop the pair had held together as moneychangers, though it is worth noting the scribe probably intended "fī al-ṣayārīf" as a locational reference. For example, this phrase may connote "fī [wakālat] al-ṣayārīf", a large commercial cooperative building in downtown Cairo, near the Jewish quarter, in which sarrafs held individual shops by the eighteenth century (Raymond, Artisans et Comerçants, Vol. I, 336-337, 376). As per the terms of the debt settlement, Yiṣḥaq b. David al-Kohen agrees to repay his former partner the rather large sum of 75 gold ashrafī in monthly installments of 3 ashrafī (25 months) starting in the month of Kislev (5325 AM). There are additional notes below this court record related to the same case, comprising an unfinished draft of the next entry in the register record #68, where another debt, of 100 [ashrafī] jadīd, is listed with a two-month repayment period that ends in Ḥeshvan (right before the one described here in record #67 is set to begin at 3 ashrafī per month). MCD.

description:
The upper part of recto is a Hebrew panegyric in praise of a scholar named Yiṣḥaq. The other text blocks are all drafts of a legal document or documents in Judaeo-Arabic. They are all quite vague and the text is damaged throughout. It seems that no names are preserved; the scribe uses "fulān" instead of names, but the other elements of the story are specific enough that these must be drafts of specific documents rather than generic formularies. 

The right side of recto mentions messengers including from the sultan; a group of "strangers" (ghurabāʾ); the synagogue; seeking permission from an "elder" regarding this matter but receiving no response (wa-anfadhū rasūl qāṣid min jihat rasūl al-sulṭān wa-min jihat al-ghurabāʾ yastaʾdhinū al-shaykh fī dhālika fa-lam yarudd lanā jawāb); and a speaker who requests to hear testimony from a group of other people. 

The left side of recto may be the response of those people ("when we were asked concerning this, we the undersigned. . ."). 

Verso begins a new legal document, probably related to the ones on recto. Refers to "the elder"; a dispute; possibly someone who apostasized (alladhī afshaʿa), and "the rayyis." 

Needs further examination.

Legal record (#71) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 23v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dating: 6 Kislev 5324 AM (1563 CE). Employment agreement, in which Farjallah b. Yehuda ha-Levi agrees to hire the boy (al-walad) ʿAbd al-Daʾīm b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Fulādī every Friday until Shevat 5325 AM. The type of employment is not stated but the daily wage is listed in two stages: 3 medin per day until Shevat 5324 (for two months) and then a pay-raise of 4 medin until Shevat 5325 AM (one year). Given that ʿAbd al-Daʾīm is mentioned as a minor and represented by his father in this agreement, it's possible that this employment arrangement was an apprenticeship. For a Rabbanite early modern document in this genre that also includes a pay raise, see: ENA NS 29.19 (PGPID 11735). This legal record (#71) includes the stipulation that Farjallah "will not let him (ʿAbd al-Daʾīm) leave/exit for the stated period of time except for the reason of excusal (בעדר // بعذر // bi-ʿudhr)." This arrangement seems to give Farjallah the authority to release the boy from employment: perhaps in the event that the potential apprenticeship was not going well. MCD.

Legal record (#73) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on ff. 24v-25v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 11 Iyyar 5325 AM (1565 CE) in the opening lines, but the latest court session mentioned is 23 Iyyar. Complex and detailed court case regarding the rumors that are circulating about the conduct of Raḥel bt. ʿAbd al-Maʿṭī al-Fūlādī, Reʾuben b. ʿAbd al-Maqṣūr al-Kohen al-parnas, and an unnamed Rabbanite man– some of which took place on the second night of Passover (a few weeks before this court record was drawn up). The case begins with the appearance of Raḥel's husband Hārūn b. Abd al-Ḥaqq al-Mawardī before the judges and community members in a court session at Bayt Simḥa (Dār Simḥa Synagogue). He "asks... for judgment" (וטלב ... לדין) to be rendered and then swears on the Ten Commandments (אלעשרת דברות). He stands before the court in disagreement with a certain Hārūn b. Yosef al-Kurdī, who Hārūn b. ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq claims has been making "excessive and deficient statements" about his wife in front of another community member, Yosef b. ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Ḥawwāsh. Hārūn b. Yosef al-Kurdī then testifies that he heard the rumors from: Hārūn b. ʿAbd al-Laṭīf al-Ḥawwāsh and Ṣedaqa b. Yosef al-Naqqāsh.

Ṣedaqa b. Yosef al-Naqqāsh then testifies before the court about a conversation he overheard between Raḥel and Reʾuben b. ʿAbd al-Maqṣūr al-Kohen al-parnas, who were speaking to each other "in the dark" somewhere on al-Sīrja Street (זקאק אלסירגה) on the second night of Passover. Some of the keywords in Ṣedaqa's testimony are unclear (ll. 14-18), but he overheard Reʾuben say: "bring me the half you have now and the half from earlier." The judges then ask Reʾuben to confirm and explain this demand, he states: "yes, I said to her bring me half the bread-dough from this time and the other half from earlier." The court record then specifies that Reʾuben was working on the "production of unleavened bread" (מן צנאע אלפטיר). The legal issue at stake seems to be whether a transaction took place on the second night of Passover– with Raḥel and Reʾuben admitting before the court that a purchase occurred between them.

The second allegation/rumor against Raḥel is brought by Hārūn b. ʿAbd al-Laṭīf al-Ḥawwāsh, who testifies that he was in Dammūh and entered the home of Raḥel's husband– where he saw people getting drunk and a Rabbanite man among the group. While Raḥel's husband was "playing ʿoud and singing," Hārūn b. ʿAbd al-Laṭīf al-Ḥawwāsh testifies that he saw her "sitting alone with the Rabbanite man," who then proceeded to "place his hand on her leg" (ואלרבאן //יחט// אידה עלי רגלהא). The judges ask Raḥel about this matter; she rejects the allegation. Community members in attendance are then asked for individual testimony, with some of them calling for the issuance of a ḥerem (בעץ מן אלגמא׳ קאלו ללדיינים אטלקו חרם). The first page of this case thus ends and it appears the second page was intentionally cut out, with only a thin stub visible along the binding.

The case continues onto the final page days after the court session one took place on 11 Iyyar. It seems likely that the missing/cutout page contained portions from the first and second sessions given that this final section mentions a brief third session (undated on a Thursday) and possibly a fourth session on the evening of Thursday 23 Iyyar. Witnesses appear before the court to provide additional and, at times, conflicting testimony. For example, Ibrahīm al-Fūlādī testifies (ll. 19-21) that he entered the home of Hārūn b. Abd al-Ḥaqq al-Mawardī that night, saw the host Hārūn playing ʿoud, but did not see the Rabbanite man there (ולם ראה אלרבאן). In the end Raḥel swears that everything disparaging being said about her, both "in Dammuh and elsewhere," is false. Her husband Hārūn testifies in the closing lines that "in his heart he is reassured/put at ease" about his wife's conduct and "does not have any doubt in her" (וליס ענדי פיהא לא ריב). MCD.

description: Legal record (#74) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 25v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated on the same "evening, month, and year" as the previous entry, so probably 23 Iyyar 5325 AM (1565 CE): which is the latest court session mentioned in the previous entry (PGPID 41533). Location/Venue: Dār Simḥa Synagogue in Cairo. In this follow-up document, Hārūn b. Abd al-Ḥaqq al-Kohen known as al-Mawardī makes an oath on the Ten Commandments in connection with the complex legal case (record #73) regarding rumors that spread about a gathering he hosted in Dammūh. The rumors centered on his wife's conduct with a Rabbanite man while Hārūn was playing ʿoud and entertaining guests. In this follow-up document, Hārūn swears that for "the rest of his life he will not return to playing ʿoud nor harp nor any other instrument from all the instruments of [musical] entertainment, not in his house nor the house of a Rabbanite nor the house of a Christian nor the house of Muslim." The oath proceeds to include other locational stipulations (within or oustide Dammūh) and perhaps stipulations related to clothing, given the mention of a fustān/dress (but possibly a specific location [bay]t fustān?). Some of these keywords are effaced or crossed out in line 16: ".[.].. ולא פי [[..ת]] פסתאן ולא פי." The end of the document mentions that this oath "is because he is a Kohen and it is upon him to maintain the proper conduct/requirements of Kohens" (לאגל אנה כהן ועליה חפט' שרוט אלכהנה). MCD.

description: Legal record (#76) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 26v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 5 Tammuz 5325 AM (1565 CE). Purchase agreement between Yehuda b. Moshe and Avraham b. David ha-Levi Shaykh al-Yahūd, in which the latter party sells "חזקת גמעה פי כנס סוק אלצאגה" (l. 3). The exact meaning of what Yehuda b. Moshe is purchasing is unclear, but it relates to the sweeping (כנס) of the Goldsmiths Market (סוק אלצאגה) in Cairo. It is unclear what the intended meaning of גמעה is here, perhaps "Friday sweeping" privileges in the market, but the object of the sale may also be material (perhaps access to sweeping equipment?). It is worth noting that the "sweepers of the market" (אלכנאסין אלסוק) are referred to collectively in line 15 and there is a clause in ll. 18-19 mentioning the weighing of shares and involvement of "a Muslim or Christian or Rabbanite." The seller Avraham al-Levi is involved in another transaction in the same court register that deals with sweeping in the Goldsmiths Market in February 1565 CE (PGPID 41599). Requires further examination. MCD.

description: Legal record (#77) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 27r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated Av 5325 AM (1565 CE). Purchase and profit-sharing agreement related to a civet cat (קט זבאד) that Ṣedaqa b. Yosef aka al-Naqqāsh bought from the seller Yaʿīsh b. ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Kohen aka al-Mawardī. The total price for the civet cat is listed as 35 gold ashrafī, a substantial sum of money. It does not seem that the buyer will take possession of the animal in order to care for it because one clause states that it will be left with Yaʿīsh, who agrees to provide it "food and drink" and to pay Ṣedaqa monthly installments of 28 medin, a sum "that corresponds to the profit that emerges from the civet cat" (ודלך פי נציר אלרבח אלדי יטלע פי אלקט אלזבאד). This debt is upon Yaʿīsh "whether [the civet cat] dies or lives" (ואן מאת ואן עאש עלי דמת יעיש). Lastly, the agreement states that the rest of the monthly profit "exceeding or less than" 28 medin will go to Yaʿīsh, the animal's caretaker. MCD.

description:
Verso: Various jottings in Arabic script. There are eight renditions of an ex libris (min kutub) for Murhaf Ibn Munqidh. There is also a snippet from an order of payment (yadfaʿ al-shaykh. . .) and an entry that looks like it contains numbers or a date.

This Murhaf is very likely to be the son of the famous Usāma Ibn Munqidh (Munqidh was the family name rather than the father's name), an Ayyubid amīr active in this period (d. 613 AH = 1216/17 CE). Murhaf signed a transmission authorization note for his father's manuscript Kitāb al-Iʿtibār in 1213 CE (RBME Árabe 1947, available at https://rbme.patrimonionacional.es/s/rbme/item/15556), but that manuscript is a later copy, likely late 13th or early 14th century (Paul Cobb, "Contemplating Books with Usāma ibn Munqidh’s Book of Contemplation," in Bestsellers and Masterpieces, ed. Blurton and Reynolds (2022), 26). Murhaf was also a known bibliophile with a large library, and the ex libris here appears to match the examples from other works belonging to him. See Ahmad Abd al-Baset, "Maktabat Murhaf b. Usāma b. Munqidh," Journal of the Institute of Arab Manuscripts [Arabic], 65, no. 1 (2021): 164–209. 

Information from Alan Elbaum, Stephanie Luescher, and Paul Cobb.

description:
Deed of purchase of a house in Jerusalem, from the Muslim court of Jerusalem.

The buyer is Yūsf b. ʿAbd al-Ghaffār b. ʿAbd al-Karīm, the Qaraite Jew, on behalf of his brother, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. This ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz is known from other contemporaneous documents, and Jerusalem Sijil records, as the person in charge of Qaraite endowments in Jerusalem from the 1560s onwards (see PGPID 40644). His son took the same position towards the end of the century.

The sellers are Ibrāhīm b. Farjallah, the Qaraite Jew, the Jewller (al-Ṣāʾigh), and ʿAbd al-Karīm b. Mūsā b. ʿAbd al-Latīf, the Qaraite Jew, the physician (al-ṭabīb). Both are known from mid-sixteenth century records in the Sijil of the Jerusalem Muslim court as the persons in charge of Qaraite endowments in Jerusalem.

The property purchased is described as located in Jerusalem (al-Quds al-Sharīf), in the Qaraite neighborhood (bi-maḥalat al-qarāʾīn). It is located above two other properties - its northern part is above the house of Ibn Zaytūn al-Yahūdī, and its southern part is above the bakery known as the bakery of the Jews (furn al-yahūd). These are also its boundaries from the south and north, and in those sides are the two gates of the propery. From east and west are publich roads.

This same property is described as a Qaraite endowment in a Jerusalem Muslim court deed from 1563 CE (PGPID 40644). In another deed, from 1583, the same property is also described as endowed by ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. ʿAbd al-Ghaffār already in 1559 CE (PGPID 40646). This means that the property puchased in 1554 as described in the deed at hand, was endowed 5 years later. 

The price paid is 60 gold Sultānīyya. 

On the verso side in a confirmation of the deed, from 14 Rajab 961 AH (15.6.1554 CE).
Also on verso, top margin, a diagonal archival note in Judeo-Arabic "deed of the second story, Jerusalem" (ḥujjat ṭabāq al-quds, חגה טבאק אלקדס ).

Recto: work on masora in Hebrew. 

Verso: Accounts in Arabic script. One section is headed Friday (yawm al-jumʿa). Mentions commodities and quantities (qadaḥ, ūqiya). The bottom section is probably headed "al-jumla."

Recto: Letter or petition in Judaeo-Arabic. Goitein suggests that it was written to the judge Avraham b. Natan, who reused it for the account on verso. The sender is a woman. Only the first part of each line is preserved, so it is difficult to understand the content. It seems that her husband has been traveling for over a year while she remains at home. It seems that some people wanted to manumit the daughter of a female slave (fa-rāmū ʿitq ibnat al-jā[riya]). Only fragmentary phrases are preserved out of the next section: the number 10; someone testifying "about her"; "her document"; the court; "the remainder of the ketubba"; "she entered the house"; and "the first."

The margin contains an extended dialogue between the speaker and a man, presumably her husband: "I said to him, 'You returned(?) [...], and the sign is our reconciliation and my demanding the ketubba from you,' and he said, 'I know that, but we will take you(?),' and I said to him by way of rejecting him/this, 'I have no replacement.' He said, 'If . . . from your dower (mahr). . . .'

description: Legal record (#78) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 27r-v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 3 Av 5325 AM (1565 CE). description: Letter from somebody in Qūṣ to a family member named Ibrāhīm b. Wāfī, in Alexandria. In Judaeo-Arabic. Dating: 11th–13th century. The beginning is missing. The preserved text begins: "nothing but terrible rumors regarding the enemy, may God bring us good news concerning you. I am in health, thank God, in Qūṣ. The only travel remaining is the journey down to you, God willing." The reference to the "enemy" is intriguing, maybe a reference to the siege of Alexandria in 1167 or 1174. The next lines are damaged but they mention Asad (unless this says li-aḥad), Fustat, Bū l-Ḥasan, and sending a letter of blame. The sender repeats that he is prepared to travel but has not yet set out from Qūṣ. Greetings to the father, to Yiṣḥaq and Bū l-Ḥasan "and my sisters and their children." Also to Maʿānī and "my paternal uncle Yosef and his children and my (grand)mother (sittī) and my paternal uncle Mufaḍḍal."
Recto, left side and verso, right side: Distribution list for clothing, including for several widows and orphans, in a different hand than the other pages.

description:
Verso, left side:
The last page contains a collection of legal statements made by different people to someone investigating what happened with a sum of money. Written in a different hand than the other pages. The beginning is missing. The first speaker says something about "from Qūṣ and down" and that "I paid the aforementioned sum to them. . . above Qūṣ. I paid the aforementioned sum to the gentile." Then Abū l-Maḥāsin al-Ṣayrafī al-Tifʾeret says that he met with al-Shaykh al-Muhadhdhab, who told him that Hiba came and said that a gentile came who "knew the location of Abū l-Fakhr, and we loaned(?) the gentile 20 dinars." (The writer inserts here "just like his brother mentioned earlier.") However, it was also "said to us" that this gentile was never acquainted with Abū l-Fakhr and did not go up to Qūṣ and did not know where Abū l-Fakhr was. Rather, Abū l-ʿAlāʾ Ibn Sakkāk is the one who knows him. Then this speaker says "I met after this with al-Muhadhdhab and told him what Hiba said to me, and he (al-Muhadhdhab) said, 'Even if the gentile wasn't the one who went up to Qūṣ, he must have heard about Abū l-Fakhr.' I asked al-Muhadhdhab about the gold, and he said, 'It's with me, by way of deposit for the gentile, and I haven't yet paid it to him, not until Abū l-Majd comes.' I met with Munā b. Tamīm who said to hme that he was sitting at the gate, and al-Muhadhdhab went up to the house. . . ." It cuts off here.

Legal record (#82) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 28v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 29 Av 5325 AM (1565 CE). Dispute following the death of Estīta bt. Farjallah al-Kohen aka al-Shuqayr, who had been betrothed to a certain ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Khiḍr al-Fūlādī. The deceased woman's father appears before the court in order to demand the return of the dowry he had given ʿAbd al-Raḥmān while his daughter was still alive, consisting of gold ashrafī jadīd coinage and a ring weighing two mithqāl. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān then states that he used the money to purchase "items for the aforementioned [Estīta]" (אלפלוס אלדי אעטיהם לי אשתרית בהם חואיג ללמד׳). ʿAbd al-Raḥmān proceeds to turn over these items and, based on their valuation, the presiding judge determines that the fiancé of the deceased woman still owes 3 ashrafī jadīd, which he commits to repay within three months. Interestingly, Farjallah allows ʿAbd al-Raḥmān to keep the gold ring he had provided as part of his daughter's dowry. MCD.

description: Legal record (#83) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 29r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 17 Elul 5325 AM (1565 CE). Marital dispute case resulting in the divorce of Avraham b. David al-Levi and Hanā bt. Moshe al-Maghribī. The record notes that a "quarrel and beating" took place between the couple and, thus, Avraham grants his wife a divorce. Based on the case's structure, Avraham may have sworn an oath in a previous marital dispute resolution or in their betrothal/ketubba conditions that if he raised a hand to his wife ever again, then she would be able to seek a divorce in court. Hanā, in turn, releases her husband from the obligations of returning her dowry and trousseau items. The record then notes, somewhat abruptly, that a quantity of wine was received by the Dār Simḥa Synagogue. This was likely a fine that Avraham had to pay for breaking the terms of a previous dispute resolution or betrothal (akin to PGPID 41609, for example). In early modern Karaite geniza documents, these penalties more commonly appear as contributions/fines of olive oil to the Dār Simḥa Synagogue. MCD.

description:
Legal record (#84) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 29r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 6 Tishrei 5325 AM (1565 CE). The year recorded by the scribe is surprising given that the previous entry on the same page is from Elul 5325, the final month of the calendar, which leads to the expectation of an entry a few weeks later in Tishrei 5326 AM rather than a chronological leap backwards of one entire year (though the next entry on the verso is indeed circa 5325). This is shift in time represents another example of the court scribe completing register entries in a non-sequential manner.

In this brief court register entry, ʿAbd al-Maʿaṭī b. Khiḍr al-Fūlādī testifies that for the rest of his life he will not seek to remarry his ex-wife, Sarah bt. Hārūn al-Qudsī. The couple divorced earlier that same day: 6 Tishrei. The record contains a clause that "he did not divorce her in [the courts] of the Jews or the Muslims," which in this context probably implies [Rabbanite] Jews– given that ʿAbd al-Maʿaṭī is testifying before a Karaite court. MCD.

The terms of repayment are uncommon, with ʿAbd al-Raḥīm committing to repay the sum on a daily basis with 1 niṣf fiḍḍa/day. Given that the couple is not seeking a divorce, the potential repayment of Sitt al-Ahl's dowry raises the question of whether her husband had misused it in some way (but the exact terms of this debt settlement remain unclear given how much is crossed out). Legal record (#89) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on ff. 30v-31r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 24 Kislev 5325 AM (1564 CE). Dispute resolution related to the betrothal and engagement of Trkīye (תרכיה) bt. Farjallah b. Naṣrallah al-Levi al-Qayyīm, whose father Farjallah had reached an agreement with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Khiḍr al-Fūlādī for her future marriage to ʿAbd al-Daʾīm (the latter's son). This agreement is alleged to have taken place two years ago, but Farjallah now claims he never swore an oath for this betrothal. Furthermore, the court notes that Trkīye and ʿAbd al-Daʾīm were both minors (ṣughār) at the time when the arrangements may have taken place. Trkīye has sinced reached maturity and is consulted by the court, stating that she is not content with the marital arrangements her father made. The case goes on to describe that Trkīye's (maternal) grandfather Shemuʾel b. Yaʿaqov al-Levi al-Somekh al-Qayyīm "wrote a fatwa" in favor of his granddaughter's position, nullifying the arrangements her father Farjallah made when she was a minor. Trkīye is consulted again by the court, again confirming her discontent with the arrangements to marry ʿAbd al-Daʾīm (who is still a minor/ṣaghīr). The court case concludes with Trkīye's engagement to a different fiancé, Yosef b. ʿAbd al-Daʾīm al-Levi al-Qudsī, who makes marital payments of: 50 silver dirham + 26 gold ashrafī + 20 gold ashrafī. Based on Trkīye's paternal nomenclature and that of her maternal grandfather (al-Levi al-Qayyīm), it is possible that her parents were paternal cousins. MCD.

There is also reference here to the involvement of a certain Ṣedaqa [no surname] and Yaʿīsh al-Kohen. Based on another entry in the same court register related to the civet business, record #77 (PGPID 41541), Ṣedaqa is likely the son of Yosef al-Naqqāsh and Yaʿīsh al-Kohen's full name is probably: Yaʿīsh b. ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Kohen aka al-Mawardī. description: Legal record (#101) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 34r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 13 Kislev 532[.] AM, with an inferred date range of 1564-1567 CE based on surrounding entries. Betrothal agreement between ʿAbd al-Jafār b. Avraham ha-Levi and Estīta bt. Shemuʾel ha-Levi. The prospective groom contributes marital payments of: 50 dirham + 30 gold ashrafī judad + 25 ashrafī judad. The marital conditions contain an unusual pledge by ʿAbd al-Jafār that he will never take a second wife who is Abyssinian or Turkish (לא חבשייה ולא תרכייא) and for 15 years he will not wed a Jewish second wife (מן בנות ישראל). The structure of this monogamy clause is rare among early modern Karaite betrothal documents, with no known parallels as of March 2026. There are also conditions against the prospective groom's travel and if he should ever curse or lay a hand to Estīta. The couple's wedding date is set two years in advance, on Second Purim (probably 27-28 Adar). The Jewish community of Cairo had recently begun to observe this communal celebration each year following the events of 1524 CE, when a rogue Ottoman governor persecuted the community and was later deposed by loyalist imperial forces. These events were recounted each year with the reading of the Megillat Miṣrayim. NB: Second Purim was also observed during the medieval period, following the events of 1012 CE (PGPID 37965, PGPID 37958), but the extent to which it was observed in early modern Cairo requires further research. MCD.

description: Recto: Fragment of a prayer for Jewish burials that was recorded on the back of a letter in Arabic c. 1708 CE (See separate record: PGPID 32488). In the introduction to her edition, Jane Hathaway notes: "On the recto of this document is the Tsiddūḳ ha-Dīn (literally, ‘affirmation of the [divine] decree’), a traditional Jewish burial prayer compiled from various verses in the Hebrew Tana"kh along with brief passages from the rabbinical oral tradition.... This Tsiddūḳ ha-Dīn is the Sephardic version, which differs considerably from its Ashkenazi counterpart in the biblical verses it includes. Both versions contain Deut. 32.4, beginning ‘The Rock, his work is perfect’, but whereas this verse opens the Ashkenazi prayer, it does not appear in the Sephardic prayer until the fifth stanza and is followed by a brief midrashic passage and one from the Mishnah. In this document, however, the stanza beginning with Deut. 32.4 follows two interpolated lines, Ps. 89.49 and Ps. 144.4, that do not form part of the conventional Sephardic Tsiddūḳ ha-Dīn." description:
Glossary of phrases in parallel Judaeo-Arabic and a Judaeo-Turkic language. The latter is not based in Ottoman Turkish, but possibly Old Uzbek and/or Chagatai. Given that Uzbek descended linguistically from Chagatay, there are a variety of shared grammatical forms to consider and this fragment may be a transitional grammatical text. Dating: probably no earlier than 13th century on paleographic grounds and likely no later than 16th century. Genre: The glossary could be a learners' text/primer based on the practical nature of its phrases. Written in a distinctive hand (with high chance of joins). The speaker uses terms of patronage in reference to an addressee (in Judaeo-Arabic): מא אחסן וגהך יא סידי . . . יא סדי אנת סידי ומכדומי . . . אקרי ממאליכך. He specifically says "give me my salary" and "do not neglect my rights" (אעטיני גאמכיתי . . . לא תפרט פי חקי). The corresponding Turkic phrase follows the second-person imperative form in Chagatay (-gil): "vergil" בירגיל ("do give" me my salary). (András Bodrogligeti, A Grammar of Chagatay, 177). The second-person imperative form -gil also exists in some early Ottoman Turkish texts (Korkut Buğday, Literary Ottoman, 17).

The first-person singular pronoun "men" (מן) is used throughout instead of "ben", an archaic feature of early Ottoman Turkish texts that is otherwise common in Uzbek, Chagatay, and other Turkic languages. For example in line 3 on the verso: (men nicesen) איש כנת אנא : מן ניגיסן -- is an unclear interrogative phrase, possibly translating idiomatically as "what/how much did you have for me?" The next bilingual phrase is damaged, but could be interrelated, ending in: .n yarım sen (".. you half"). The first line of the verso, contains the clearly rendered phrase: bir safar qīlūrman ביר ספר קילורמן ("I will go on a trip"), which bears evidence of the Uzbek future first-person indefinite conjugation -arman/-urman for the verb qilmoq (to do). This conjugation form does not exist in Ottoman Turkish. https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Appendix:Uzbek_verbs // https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/qilmoq 

On the recto, the first legible phrase pairing reads: ולא מסאפר: מן ספרכא... (men safarga). This construction seems to draw on the Uzbek and/or Chagatay dative case -ga, yielding the partial translation "I am on a trip," though the equivalent negation (as ולא) is missing along the paper tear. The dative suffix -ga is also repeated in l. 10 of the recto (חקינכא). For a full overview of relevant case suffixes, see: https://www.turkolog.ist/uzbek/Uzbek_cases.pdf // Bodrogligeti, 33-34

Another phrase on the recto reads: לא תר.. חתי אגי // אכיתמאס כלינגא -- "do not (verb) until I arrive/come." Although the verb stem's meaning is unclear, it might bear the Uzbek indefinite future negation suffix -mas (akitmās gelence/agitmās gelence). Chagatay features a verbal negation suffix -mas for the Aorist present tense (Bodrogligeti, 204). (Identified by Alan Elbaum and Matthew Dudley)

The contemporary historian Muḥsin ʻAlī Shūmān has found evidence in Ottoman qadi court records that a wave of Jewish refugees arrived in Cairo from Central Asia in the early 1600s, naming Uzbekistan as one of the potential points of emigration. (The Jews in Ottoman Egypt Until the Beginning of the Nineteenth Century/al-Yahūd fī Miṣr al-ʻUthmānīyah ḥattá awāʾil al-qarn al-tāsiʻ ʻashar, vol. II, 361-363). For an early modern geniza fragment mentioning someone who is "from Samarqand," in modern-day Uzbekistan, see the following Ladino accounts: T-S AS 209.112 (PGPID 39773)

description: Legal record (#107) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 35v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 27 Kislev 5326 AM (1565 CE). Betrothal agreement between the prospective bride and groom Yiṣḥaq b. ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Kohen al-Kurdī and Estīta bt. Shimʿon ha-Levi ha-Ḥazzan (who is probably represented by her father). The wedding date is set for the following year. The groom's payments are listed as: 50 dirham + 30 ashrafī judad. The betrothal agreement lists a fine that Yiṣḥaq must pay his wife if he ever strikes her and a clause restricting his travel outside Miṣr/מצר (Egypt or possibly Cairo). Estīta may have been a minor at the time of this agreement because the travel prohibition clause might read: "except by consent of the [bride's] fa[ther?]" (these clauses are normally framed by the bride's legal consent) MCD.

description: Legal record (#109) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 36r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 17 Shevat 5326 AM (1566 CE). Brief entry stating that Farjallah b. ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Kohen Shuqayr and [...] bt. Yiṣḥaq Fayrūz married each other before two witnesses, but this is clearly not a ketubba nor does it follow common formulae in other entries from the same court register (except the neighboring record #110). These two documents may be in a distinct scribal hand compared to nearby entries on surrounding folios. Intriguingly, the scribe notes that the "ʿāqid (rabbi officiant) was Moshe ha-Nashiyā in the residence of the Rabbanite Ibn Ṣor [located] at the start of al-Mudawwar Street." Although none of the people named directly in the entry are Rabbanite, it seems that wedding may have taken place in a property owned by a Rabbanite community member in Cairo. For other references to the street Darb al-Mudawwar in the city's Jewish quarter, see: Yevr.-Arab. II 1389 (PGPID 27932), Yevr.-Arab. II 1398 (PGPID 27940). MCD.
scholarship_records: Matthew Dudley's digital edition (2026).

description: Legal record (#110) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 36r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Yosef al-Levi married each other before two witnesses, but this is clearly not a ketubba nor does it follow common formulae in other entries from the same court register (except the neighboring record #109). The groom's payments are listed as: 50 dirham + 200 medin + 1,000 medin. The closing lines note that the ʿāqid (rabbi officiant) was Shemuʾel ha-Dayyan, one of the Karaite judges known from other entries, and that the wedding took place in the residence of Shemuʾel al-Fūlādī. description:
Legal record (#111) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 36v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 10 Iyyar 5327 AM (1567 CE). Rental agreement for a property held in the Karaite pious endowment of Cairo. ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Ḥakīm b. Yehuda ha-Rofe ha-dayyan appears before Shemuʾel ha-dayyan, in the latter's own home, in order to rent a portico (riwāq) property. There is an interlinear addition above l. 5 that pours over into the margin which helps contextualize the meaning of riwāq, at term that might not literally mean "portico" as is conventionally translated because a shop and a residence are specified: "the shop (and?) residence of Farjallah b. Yehuda al-Levi the cook (al-ṭabbakh)." 

The reference to Yehuda ha-Rofe ha-dayyan as deceased (נ׳׳ע) in his son's nomenclature is significant. This marks the first time the communal judge is listed as such in the court register after last appearing alive in July 1565 CE (legal record #79): PGPID 41550. MCD.
scholarship_records: Matthew Dudley's digital edition (2026).

description: Legal record (#112) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 36v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 16 Iyyar 5327 AM (1567 CE). Incomplete dispute resolution against further physical altercations/insults between Raḍī b. Shemuʾel Berakha and the brothers ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Shelomo, Aharon, sons of Shemuʾel al-Fūlādī and their paternal cousin ʿAbd al-Jaffār b. Farjallah al-Fūlādī. The resolution contains a variety of stipulations that the parties agree to: they will not strike, curse, capture/chase, or control one another nor will they cause anyone else to do so whether Muslim, Christian, or Jew. Surprisingly, this incomplete legal draft lists an end date for the agreement of the following holiday of Shavuʿot (rather than a ban in perpetuity). MCD.

description:
A long and flowery communal, formal letter in Hebrew, addressed to the elders of the community of Malīj, probably from the leaders of the Jewish community of Fustāt (ממנו בית דין בשפריר קבוע מבין דין הגדול נטוע וממקצת הקהל הצנוע כאהלים תקוע).

The letter is concerned with a dispute between two persons, which started in Malīj, dealt with by the elders there to the dissatisfaction of one of the parties, who then appealed to the court in Fustāt. The letter urges the local elders to reconsider the case, and especially the other party's use of non-Jewish courts. 

The letter occupies most the verso side of the manuscript. A blank space and a horizontal libe separates it from the next block of text (Reinach II).
scholarship_records: Moise Schwab, "Textes judéo-égyptiens du XIe siècle ; lettres diverses et poésies liturgiques," Revue des Etudes Juives 70 (n.p., 1920), 44-69.

description:
A letter to a certain Ḥaver, Yosef b. Ya'aqov, probably residing in Tyre.

The letter itself is in Hebrew, and inculde a long a flowery opening and blessings. Before the letter, a long title in Judeo-Arabic, in a slightly larger script, describing the letter as addressed to the above mentioned Ḥaver, as dealing with a suftaja, and mentions names of several witnesses, some of them are known merchants. 

The letter mentions three different checks (דיוקני), their authentication, documents in Arabic script (בכתב חרוט ומבוטא בלשון הגרי).

The letter occupies the lower half of recto. End is missing.

description: Piyyuṭ fragment in an exquisite scribal hand comprising a portion of the Yom ha-Kippur Amidah (per FGP). The FGP description does not reference two faint marginal notes in Latin on the recto stating the year "Anno 1624" and, a second dated note: "Bib Trinitatis 1625." The latter note may be significant for tracing the provenance of the fragment. Potential candidates for Bib[liotheca] Trinitatis in the 1620s include: Trinity College, Cambridge; Trinity Hall, Cambridge; Trinity College Dublin; Trinity College, Oxford; and perhaps other institutions. Possibly non-geniza based on the marginal notes. Requires further research. (MCD with information from Dr. Pranav Jain)

Fragments of legal queries, possibly sent together as a single letter. Dating: 16th- or 17th-century (per Glick). Location: Siderokapısı/Sidrekapsi (סידריקאפס[י]), a mining town in what is now modern-day Greece, is mentioned on the lower right edge of the recto but the context is unclear due to the extensive damage. During the Ottoman period, Siderokapısı was home to a large Jewish population with hundreds of families (Minna Rozen, The Corvée of Operating the Mines in Siderokapısı, 37, 45). 

Location: one of the legal queries on T-S Misc.28.255 was sent from Adrianople (Edirne) by Avraham b. Moshe Sabrigo (שאבריגו) and Shemuʾel ha-Kohen on behalf of the city's Portuguese congregation. The legal query bears both their autographs. Another portion of the fragment contains a letter signed by a certain Yiṣḥaq ʿOvadya, who writes about several other legal queries that do not appear on T-S Misc.28.255 but possibly once comprised additional pages to the letter. Shemuel Glick identifies Yiṣḥaq ʿOvadya as potentially the same individual who published אגרת דופי הזמן in Venice in 1598– full text available at: https://hebrewbooks.org/52557 (Information from Shmuel Glick's description/edition in FGP) 

NB: Minna Rozen lists the location of Siderokapısı as "some eight kilometers southeast of Thessaloniki," but this geographical association does not seem possible (Rozen, The Corvée of Operating the Mines in Siderokapısı, 37). The mining town in question may have been much further east in the Chalkidiki peninsula, where the Ottoman "Siderokapısı" or "Sidrekapsi" mint was also located (possibly Stratoniki, Stratoni, or Sidiriolakkos). A map of this mint's location in Şevket Pamuk's work supports the latter locations as possible candidates: Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire, 91. MCD.

Primary use (probably): Business accounts in the hand of Avraham Ibn Yijū. Concerning transactions conducted in Jurbattan in betel nut, cardamom, coins, and copper and lead. Listing travel provisions (zād) including wheat, lārī rice, local rice, oil, honey, and clarified butter. Provides values both in the Egyptian standard (mithqāls) and the local standard ("in the weight of Jurbattan"). The accounts conclude, "I gave Ashū 15 malikīs and 4 mithqāls." This is only the second known appearance of Ashū by name, and it shows that Goitein and Friedman were correct to conclude that she is the one referred to as "your house" in T-S Misc.25.103 (PGPID 4738). It is notable that Ibn Yijū continued to call her Ashū rather than the Hebrew name Berakha she took upon her manumission/conversion in 1132 (IOM D 55.10 (PGPID 5501)).

Dating: Ibn Yijū's wife and children were in Jurbattan as of 1146 based on T-S Misc.25.103. He had left India for Aden by 1149, providing a terminus ante quem. If the mention of ʿAbd Allāh in l. 2 refers to Ibn Yijū's associate the nākhudā Abū ʿAbd Allāh who died in 1146, then these accounts would date to 1146 or earlier. It is puzzling that Ibn Yijū seems to have written these brief accounts on a very large piece of paper and not to have reused the copious blank space until ~1151. But it is not implausible, given that he often reused scrap paper later for calendars and/or accounts years later. 

Identified by Alan Elbaum.

description: Legal record (#115) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 37v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated 1 Tammuz 5326 AM (1566 CE). Loan agreement and investment partnership in which Yiṣḥaq b. Moshe aka Maghribi ha-Qaraʾī receives 70 gold peraḥīm (ashrafī) from Moshe b. Meʾīr aka (name omitted). The profit from the partnership is split into two equal shares and Moshe grants Yiṣḥaq authority to utilize the funds as he sees fits in commercial transactions. There is also a stipulation that 5 of the 70 peraḥīm will remain in the hand of Moshe and, in turn, Yiṣḥaq grants him authority to transfer the funds to his wife in monthly payments of 1 peraḥ to cover "the needs of her household." This arrangement carries the implication that Yiṣḥaq will likely be traveling for business and thus needs to ensure the financial well-being of his family for five months while he is absent. MCD.

description: A defense of the pietists in Egypt, written by the Nagid in the form of a circular to the judges under his jurisdiction. At the time a number of rabbinic judges across Egypt had initiated a campaign to excommunicate and brand pietists as heretics, in response to the perceived excesses and heretical anomalies of some of them. The original accusations have not survived, but in his rejoinder the Nagid urges caution and restraint. The circular is undated, but the handwriting of the Nagid is unmistakably that of Abraham Maimonides. The document consists of forty eight lines, preceded by a title page containing another four lines. This is a draft, written in the Nagid’s own hand; he left blank spaces for the copyist to fill in the quotations from the Bible and the Talmud alluded to in the text. (Information from Goitein, “Abraham Maimonides on Pietists," Journal of Jewish Social Studies 16 (1965), 109–114 and Russ-Fishbane, Judaism, Sufism, and the Pietists of Medieval Egypt, 73–74) EMS

Legal record (#116) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 38r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). The date is damaged, with only the month of Tammuz legible. This entry could have been written around the same timespan as the previous record #115: which is dated 1 Tammuz 5326 AM (1566 CE). This legal case deals with a dispute over someone's possession of the materia medica item "China root" (smilax) or perhaps "Chinese licorice" (ʿaraq Sinī) and refers to a specific part of the plant itself (שגאף/شغاف)– which is probably some kind of membrane (the term is commonly used as "pericardium" for human anatomy). The legal case may center on disputed ownership, but much of the opening lines are lost to damage. The lower section of the record deals with a communal fine of 10 qinṭārs of olive oil (zayt ṭayyib) payable to the heqdesh of the Karaites. This is a common fine among early modern Karaite legal documents from Cairo. MCD/ASE.

For scholarship on the usage of "China root" in the sixteenth century, see: Anna E. Winterbottom, "Of the China Root: A Case Study of the Early Modern Circulation of Materia Medica," Social History of Medicine, Volume 28, Issue 1, February 2015, 22–44.

In which Moshe reports that he traveled with the aforementioned goods entrusted to him by Sason b. Natan to Upper Egypt (al-Ṣāʿīd). He sold them and purchased other commodities with the proceeds and delivered those to Sason, with no further liabilities between them. The court asked Sason to respond, who said, "Yes, I gave him saffron and yeast and various other goods documented by me (mathbūta ʿindī). When he arrived, I asked him about everything he obtained, and I saw a discrepancy. I told him, 'What you have brought me is about half of my property.' And he gave me this ruqʿa in the handwriting of Abū Isḥāq b. Ṭībān which he wrote in my absence, and he said, 'This is the correct account of everything you sent with me.'" The next two lines are difficult to read. It seems that according to this document Moshe acknowledged owing 4 dinars to Sason. Moshe then responds to the court explaining that the goods were entrusted to him by way of commenda (muḍāraba) and that he was not instructed to make purchases(?). He then wishes Sason to take an oath.

Four consecutive folios from the introduction to an anonymous philosophical-polemical treatise defending Jewish prayer and law against the criticism of Muslims. Contains the only known mention in a geniza fragment of the Fatimid vizier Yaʿqūb b. Killis. Following an ornamental proem (dībāja, literally, brocade) closely modeled on the introduction to Saʿadya Gaʾon's siddur, the author recounts how "the most illustrious vizier Yaʿqūb b. Yūsuf" (Ibn Killis), at his regular majlis where religions were discussed in the presence of littérateurs, mutakallimūn, philosophers, and physicians, displayed an Arabic-script translation of Saʿadya's siddur Kitāb Jāmiʿ al-Ṣalawāt wa-l-Tasābīḥ), whereupon he and the assembled Muslims ridiculed Jewish prayers and beliefs to the shame of the Rabbanites and Qaraites present. The author, evidently a rabbinic scholar and disciple of Saʿadya, responds by praising the excellence of Jewish law and liturgy, citing Deuteronomy 4:6–8 in Saʿadya's tafsīr. Cohen and Somekh suggest that the account corroborates Ibn Khallikān's anecdote about Ibn Killis's majlis and may even describe the same incident. They also argue that the author's decision to confront the vizier with verses from the Torah implies that he regarded Ibn Killis as still, in some sense, answerable to his origins. The blessing "may God sustain his high station" after the vizier's name indicates that Ibn Killis was alive and in office when the treatise was composed, suggesting a dating for the text of 979–91 CE. Cohen and Somekh argue that the treatise was originally written in Arabic script for a Muslim audience, and this copy is a transcription into Hebrew characters for Jewish readers, datable on paleographic grounds to the tenth or early eleventh century. Order: ENA 3734.12; ENA 2643.12; ENA 2643.11; ENA 3734.13. First two leaves ed. and trans. Mark R. Cohen and Sasson Somekh, "In the Court of Yaʿqūb Ibn Killis: A Fragment from the Cairo Genizah," JQR n.s. 80 (1990), 283–314; revised translation (given below) in Mark R. Cohen and Sasson Somekh, “Interreligious Majalis in Early Fatimid Egypt,” in Hava Lazarus-Yafeh, et al., eds., The Majlis: Interreligious Encounters in Medieval Islam (Wiesbaden: Otto Harrassowitz Verlag, 1999), 128–36. Leaves 3 and 4 edited and translated in Sasson Somekh, "Remnants of a Polemical Work from the Cairo Geniza" (Hebrew), in Sefer Shivtiel: meḥqarim ba-lashon ha-ʿivrit uve-mesorot ha-ʿedot, ed. Yitzhak Gluska and Semah Kesar (Ramat-Gan, 1992), 141–59. MR

The recto and verso of this document are both copies of the same responsum written to Avraham Maimonides. The debtor requests Avraham's intervention to secure sixty dirhems for him and to convince the creditor to change the terms of the loan from twenty to ten dirhems per month. Friedman believes the handwriting "resembles that of Elijah ben Zechariah who served as judge in Alexandria at least from 1204 and in Fustat during the years 1222–36. He was in charge of the poor and the orphans, and many petitions to him have been preserved in the Genizah, including requests that he seek Abraham Maimonides' intervention." (Information and quotation from Friedman, "Responsa of Abraham Maimonides on a Debtor's Travails")

The second note mentions the arrival of someone (a gabbay) from Livorno on the 18th, but the placename is spelled in a manner resembling the archaic title in English (Legorna=Leghorn?). Based on the honorifics, it seems possible that the surname of the gabbay included סורייה (Sūriyya)– perhaps the "De Sūriyya" or "Sūriyya" (both surnames are attested in the geniza: T-S K15.104 - PGPID 23209 // BL OR 6356.1–16 PGPID 40934). Another version of Ibn Yijū's poem in praise of Maḍmūn and cursing his enemies (India Book II, 39), in the hand of the same scribe as AIU IV.C.486 (PGPID 39481). Identification and join by Alan Elbaum with the assistance of the Dicta Genizah Search website for the MiDRASH Automatic Transcriptions (https://zenodo.org/records/17734473).

There are a few interesting variants here compared to the other copies:
- There is no header (T-S 8J16.23 starts ולה איצא ימדח סידנא מצמון נגיד עם יי)
- A trivial change of אברהם בנו יגו to אברהם נין יגו
- A significant change of the recipient: instead of בנו יפת (referring to Maḍmūn the son of Yefet) it says בנו מחפוץ ("the son of Maḥfūẓ"). In fact the paper is mildly damaged here, and the word Maḥfūẓ is squeezed into a space that is slightly too small. Looking closely, it seems possible that the scribe first wrote יפת and then changed it to the word מחפוץ. The best candidate among Ibn Yijū's associates might be Ḥalfon b. Shemarya (aka Abū Saʿīd b. Maḥfūẓ) Ibn Jumayhir; see Goitein and Friedman, India Traders, 331n13 (edition of T-S 20.130, India Book II, 20).

The lower piece was published by Allony in "משירת ספרד ולשונה," Sinai 55 (1964), 257, who did not know what to make of the name יגו and did not identify the poet.

Ownership note for a small quire: Yehuda b. Yefet ha-Levi.

From a volume of piyyuṭim. On parchment. Verso was a blank page that has been filled in with a medical prescription for chest and rib pains and an ownership note: "this belongs (or: is by?) my father, Shabbetay b. Yosef ha-Mumḥe b. Elʿazar b. Yosef b. [..]mūm(?) ha-Shofeṭ. Possibly the same man as in T-S NS 320.50c (PGPID 25428).
Literary text with ownership note: Shelomo b. Avraham ha-Shofeṭ Segulat ha-Yeshiva.
Ownership or authorship note: the noble cantor ([al-ḥazz]an al-jalīl Saʿadya b. Ṭoviyya, known as Tifʾeret ha-Ḥazzanim).
Colophon dated to a Friday in Av 1427 Seleucid = 1116 CE.
Ownership note for a literary text: the cantor Yiṣḥaq b. Ghālib ha-Ḥazzan (known from other such fragments).
Bifolio of piyyuṭ in a beautiful hand, with an ownership or authorship note: Yosef b. Ḥalfon ha-Kohen.
Dedication note for a quire of piyyuṭim for "the dear boy" Nafīs b. Abū Ṭāhir. Beautiful calligraphy.

Poem אברך אל אשר יצר יצורים ואודהו. According to the colophon on verso, the poem is in honor of Elʿazar b. Yosef ha-Levi and was written by Menashshe b. Yehuda ‘Descendant of the Geʾonim’. A Menashshe b. Yehuda, living at the end of the 11th century, is known from other Genizah documents, though it is not clear whether this is the same figure. (Information from CUDL.)
Ownership or authorship note: Abū l-Bishr Sulaymān b. Moshe ha-Levi.
Ownership or authorship note: Ḥalfon b. Sheʾerit b. Yaʿaqov.
Ownership note: Aharon b. Peraḥya.

Piyyuṭim by Samuel the Third, pertaining to Parashat Vayeḥi (Genesis 47:28-50:26). F. 2r contains most of the ofan; f. 2v contains the meʾora and the first part of the ahava; f. 1r contains the final two lines of the מי כמוך, all of the י‫׳ מלכנו‬, and most of the ועד מתי, which concludes on f. 1v. 

F. 1v contains a colophon giving the name of the copyist (Avraham b. Aharon) and the date and place of completion of the copy (Cairo, Thursday, 14 Av 1406 of the Seleucid Era (= 1095 CE)).

(Information from CUDL.)

Upper half of a Hebrew letter addressed to the majlis of (the Nagid) Abū Zikrī (Yehuda) b. Saʿadya. Address in Judaeo-Arabic on verso. Written in an elevated register. Likely a request for assistance of some kind. There are good chances of finding a join.
Quire of piyyuṭim containing a note "Berakhot b. Yefet wrote this for himself."

Letter fragment in Judaeo-Arabic. Late. Addressed to ʿOvadya in Fustat (Miṣrayim) in the neighborhood of the Qaraites (חרות(!) אלקראין). The origin seems to appear in the address but is unclear (מן אלמנטייה?) or possibly אלמנשייה المنشية, which could refer to a specific part of Alexandria or a variety of small towns near Acre, Safed, Tulkarm, and Jenin. Mentions someone named Shtīwī; contains greetings; "when I traveled from the city"; and Sulaymān.
Ownership note: Shemuʾel b. Ṭoviyya ha-Levi. Also mentions Tammuz and [...] b. Netanʾel ha-Ḥazzan in a colophon(?) above.
Ownership notes: Tiqva b. [...]; Yosef b. Tiqva; Tiqva b. Yefet b. Yosef (and a b. Yehuda has been added after this in a different hand).
Ownership note: Abū l-Faḍl Ibn al-Dimyāṭī.
Small fragment of an Arabic legal deed, probably a Muslim marriage contract (...الصداق المذكور...).

Verso, left: beginning of a genealogical list for "the house of the learned judge": Saʿadya and his six sons, beginning with Shemuʾel the judge (al-dayyan al-maskil... ha-dayyan ha-ḥakaham ha-niflaʾ...). Parts of this text are repeated twice below, with spelling mistakes. Verso, right: jottings in Arabic and Hebrew scripts. Recto: Judaeo-Arabic commentary on Tosefta, Beraḵot 1:1, with biblical quotations. (Information in part from CUDL.)
Book of oneiromancy in Judaeo-Arabic attributed to Ibn Sirīn.
Ownership note: Moshe b. Ṭoviyyahu he-Ḥaver ha-Kohen.

Bifolio of accounts in Judaeo-Arabic and some Arabic, probably of a grocer. Mentions items including sesame oil, hazelnut, sugar, bread, cheese, rice, sumac, ʿaqīd of almond (though this is written out לוז עקיד rather than עקיד לוז), rose, cucumber, apple, an ublūja of sugar, pomegranate seeds. Mentions people such as Ṣibyān; Ibn al-Ramlī; the beadle of the synagogue (khādim al-kanīs); the clothier (al-bazzāz) Abū l-ʿAysh; the house of Abū l-Faḍl.
Ownership note for Yeḥezqel b. ʿEli he-Ḥaver ha-Kohen. At the bottom of the page there are also two lines in Arabic script.

Bifolio of accounts in Judaeo-Arabic and some Arabic. Organized in part by parshiyot (CUDL suggests that the sums mentioned could be an auction for the rights to read the parshiyot). Mentions names such as Abū Naṣr al-Dallāl; Munajjā; Abū l-Faḍl; al-Shaykh al-Rashīd Ibn al-[...]. Other entries include "when I arrived from Bilbays"; a mention of kāmilī dirhams (first minted in 1225); chicken; wood; ṭaḥīna; qaṭāra.
Verso: Drafts of phrases from a letter in Hebrew, Judaeo-Arabic, and Arabic, including one addressed to Rabbenu Tamīm ha-Kohen.
Ownership note: Naḥum b. Yosef.

Maimonides, Mishne Tora, Hilkhot Sheviṭat ʿAsor 3:2-10, dated in the colophon on f. 1v-2r to 17 Ṭevet 1769 of the Seleucid Era (= 1458 CE). The scribe's name has been rubbed out. (Information from CUDL.)

Formal letter from the office of Maṣliaḥ Gaʾon, whose name and genealogy appear at the top, in addition to משער הישיבה in the address on verso. Addressed to Abū Saʿd b. Khallūf in Fuwwa. Summoning him, probably to appear before the court ("without any protest") for something to do with Hiba b. Manṣūr the ḍāmin of dyeing 'in it' (= in Fuwwa?).

A practice run and the final version of an inscription mentioning the qodesh of the community of ʿAbbāsiyya and the name Isaac Sāhayl (סאהיל). Late. ʿAbbāsiyya is one Cairo's neighborhoods but the fragment might refer to a different location. (Information in part from CUDL.)

Colophon commemorating the presence in ‘this noble place’ of Elʿazar b. Avraham b. Shānjū Isaiah(?) (שאנגו יזייא) on Sunday, the Eve of Yom Kippur of 5392 A.M. (= October, 1631 CE). Various other names are written between the lines and in the top and bottom margins of the colophon, including Yehuda b. Shush ha-Levi, Yosef ha-Levi, David ha-Levi, Moses ha-Levi, David Duqis, Yaʿaqov […], Mordehai, Eliyya, Ḥalfon b. Moshe, Elʿazer b. Pesaḥ Ashkenazi, Moshe Bālansi, and Avraham Kohen. Some of these names are repeated a number of times. (Information mainly from CUDL.)

Ownership notes stating that the codex (מצחף) belongs to Shelomo b. Mevasser b. Sahl ha-ʿAnī. A later ownership note added below the original text states that the book now belongs to Sibāʿ b. Moshe ha-Levi and his two sons, Efrayim and Menashshe. Writing exercises with the beginning of the Hebrew alphabet in the top margin. Solomon b. Mevasser b. Sahl ha-ʿAnī is also known from T-S 24.7 (dated 1003–4 CE), which is a Qaraite ketubba for his marriage to his cousin. (Information from CUDL.)

A copy of the authorisation by Egyptian Jewish authorities of Avraham Maimonides’ enactment concerning procedures for issuing a ban of excommunication. Dated ḥol ha-moʿed of Passover 1546 of the Seleucid Era (= April, 1235 CE). Includes the authorisations by Shelomo b. Yishay Nesi ha-gola, Peraḥya b. Yosef the judge, Ahuv b. Yosef, Yiṣḥaq b. Avraham Sefaradi, Yoshiyya Nasi b. Yishay Nasi. At the bottom of the current recto there are pen trials. (Information from CUDL.)

End of a prayer with a colophon. According to the colophon, the prayer was written by a person whose name is hidden in the series of letters נכמפט ha-Kohen for Yosef, Yiṣḥaq and ʿEli, sons of Yaʿaqov b. ʿAmran. The hidden name is an atba''sh for טליון, Ṭalyon, a shortened version of Avṭalyon. Next to the colophon, there is a blessing in a different hand and ink for Parḥon b. Yosef. In the bottom part of verso and on recto is Leviticus 1:1–8. (Information from CUDL.)
Ownership notes: Yiṣḥaq b. Avraham b. Yiṣḥaq b. Avraham b. Yiṣḥaq b. Avraham b. Daniʾel b. Yiṣḥaq. Then it was purchased by Avraham b. Yaʿaqov Darʿī.
Recto: Medical prescriptions in Judaeo-Arabic. Verso refers to Sayyidnā al-Nagid and a line about the laws of Sheḥiṭa by the late Rabbenu Moshe (Maimonides). Hand of Shelomo b. Eliyyahu?

Jeremiah 31:35–36. 

Above and between the two verses remains of a (legal?) text in faded ink are visible that include the words פרוטה and י״ב זוזים. At the bottom of the page, the names Hiba b. Bihyā (or Bahiyya? ביהיא) and Sutayt (סותית) bt. Yaʿaqov are written in the same faded ink. (Information mainly from CUDL.)
Colophon of a book written by Shaʾul b. Avraham b. Natan for Yeḥezqel b. Maṣliaḥ b. Shela. (Information from CUDL.)
Ownership note: Ṣedaqa b. Ṣemaḥ purchased this quire.

Recto: verses in Arabic expressing the book owner’s intention to not lend his copy to anybody without making a written note of it. The first three lines are written in Arabic script, then repeated in Judaeo-Arabic. Then the next three lines are written in Arabic script but without a Judaeo-Arabic transcription, probably because the copyist ran out of space. Verso: the colophon, specifying that this is a book by Shemuʾel b. Hošaʿna (Third in the Academy), copied by Yehuda b. Yefet ha-Levi in the month of Jumādā al-Awwal, 550 of the Hijra (= July, 1155 CE). (Information from CUDL.)

At the top of recto in square letters: two unfinished lines from the beginning of Midraš Tanḥuma on the weekly portion בראשית (Genesis 1:1-6:8). This is followed by another midraš written in a more cursive hand, which is identified below the text as מדרש ללחכמים ז״ל. An ownership note states that the text belonged to Shemuʾel ha-Kohen Dallāti, with an admonition in Judaeo-Arabic that he should study it. (Information fro CUDL.)

Jottings and drawings on recto and verso, some of which are stick figures. Mentioning Avraham Meron ha-Levi, Yehuda ha-Levi, and Yaʿaqov b. Moshe. Some phrases are repeated, including משנה מקרא תלמוד, אימא לא שנא בן and שלם רב וישע יקרב … נאהב, as well as Proverbs 1:8. (Information from CUDL.)

Maimonides, Mišne Tora, closing paragraph of Sefer Zemanim (recto) and beginning of Sefer Našim (verso). A colophon in Judaeo-Arabic at the end of Sefer Zemanim states that the book was completed in II Adar of the year 5201 (= March, 1441 CE) by Naftali b. Yeshuʿa b. Yosef. [It may be dated 5231 instead, as there is a partial lacuna over the decade.] Under the colophon a legal case is described of a man and a woman who were married without realising that they had the same father. (Information mainly from CUDL.)

Recto: Torah reading for Šavuʿot: Exodus 19:1–4 with Targum Onqelos. The Hebrew text of Exodus 19:1 is written in full. Only incipits of Exodus 19:2–4 in Hebrew are included. Full text of all verses in Aramaic is included. Verso: colophon mentioning Saʿadya b. Elʿazar (owner) and Abū Saʿd ha-Levi (scribe). (Information from CUDl.)

Recto: Yehuday Gaʾon, Halaḵot Pesuqot, Hilḵot ʿEruvin. Verso: note of purchase stating that ʿAmram ha-Kohen b. Aharon ha-Kohen b. ʿAmram bought ‘Halaḵot of Yehudai Gaʾon’ from Shemuʾel ha-Kohen b. Natan ha-Kohen. The former name is surrounded with small letters, only some of which are preserved. (Information mainly from CUDL and PGP signatures database.)

Babylonian Talmud, ʿEruvin 2a-b (f. 2) and 11a–12a (f. 1). 

F. 2v contains three notes of purchase. The book was initially purchased by Menaḥem b. Shemuʾel. The second note records that the book was bought by the Palestinian Gaʾon Maṣliaḥ ha-Kohen in Kislev of the year 1448 of the Seleucid Era (= 1136 CE). This note is in the hand of Ḥalfon ha-Levi b. Menashshe and is signed by Natan b. Shelomo ha-Kohen and Ḥalfon himself. The signature of Natan b. Shelomo is surrounded by small letters indicating the date of the sale. A third note, written in a third hand, records that the book was bought by Menaḥem b. Berakhot from the estate of the gaʾon in 1457 of the Seleucid Era (= 1145 CE). (Information from CUDL.)

End of Hai Gaʾon, Kitāb Adab al-Qaḍā (‘Book of Good Manner for Legal Procedure’). Dated in the colophon to Tammuz 4835 from Creation (= 1075 CE). A barely legible note below the colophon states that the book was purchased by Yiṣḥaq b. Ḥayyim and mentions the name Yehosef ha-Levi. (Information from CUDL.)

Legal record (#122) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 40r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 27 Sivan 5329 AM (1569 CE). Partnership dissolution and settlement of debts between Manṣūr b. Yehuda al-Levi and ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. Rabbi Yehuda ha-dayyan Rofe, who had been partners with ʿAbd al-Raḥīm b. Farjallah Ḥazzan. Manṣūr and ʿAbd al-Wāḥid now form a new partnership that lays out the pair's plans for profit-sharing in the buying and selling of perfume. MCD.

description: Sequence of magical characteres in an indecipherable cipher, with corresponding signs below, including some Arabic consonants. (Information from CUDL.)
List of angels that are likely to intervene in particular circumstances. (Information from CUDL.)

Some sort of multiplication table describing the results of multiplying different orders of magnitude, e.g. "the tens with the thousands, the answer is. . ." Accompanied by numerals. Verso is not digitized (CUDL and FGP only have two images of recto). 

There is also Hebrew text with a discourse on the calendar, mentioning the different types of Hebrew year (complete, normal, defective; leap, regular) and rules for calendar reckoning. (Information in part from CUDL.)
Calendar in the hand of Yedutun ha-Levi.

Verso: One line from a state document, evidently a decree or official letter issued by the caliph al-Ḥākim: من عبد الله ووليه المنصور ابي علي الامام الحاكم بامر الله امير المومنين بن الامام العزيز بالله امير المومنين

Reused for 4 aggressive magical recipes, one to destroy a house, one to drive a person away from an apartment or a shop, and two recipes to cause hatred between two people. (Information in part from CUDL.)

Inventory or account written on an irregular piece of parchment, consisting of a long list of materia medica with their corresponding weights. Merits further examination. 

On verso there are pen trials.
A spell to silence Ibrahim b. Karīma and prevent him from thinking evil thoughts of Faḍlān b. Baghdād, and to make him return 15 dinars. (Information from CUDL.)
An amulet for Ṣadoq b. Hodaya, with the name Atniq Jalīl (אתניק גליל). Possibly also refers to Mevorakh and Abū ʿAlī as the person's enemies. (Informationf rom CUDL.)
Recto: an adjuration of demons or angels, to reveal things to Yaʿqov b. Yosef. Verso: titles of magical recipes, including one for the road and three for dream requests. (Information from CUDL.)

Formulaic phrases from the beginning of a letter to Abū l-Faraj written in a very unusual (magical?) shape. Verso contains more text written in a spiral and a drawing of something that looks like an inverted dome or a bladder.
Love spell for Dalāl bt. Ḍiyāʾ and ʿAshīr b. Waṣṣāf.
Amulet for Sahlān b. ʿAzīza.
Legal fragment in the hand of Ḥalfon b. Menashshe. Lower right corner. Mentions Sitt al-Ahl bt. [...] and a husband (Abū) l-Faraj Hibatallāh. No signatures.

Fragment of a legal document. Cryptic phrases about "releasing myself from God" and "the vicissitudes of time" and saying to a woman "you will regret. . ." Might be related to the neighboring fragments (similar state of discoloration).
Small fragment of a legal document containing only formulaic phrases. Might be related to the neighboring fragments (similar state of discoloration).

Letter in Hebrew from Moshe b. תיפא(?). The sender mentions Mordekhay Benyamin, business in Cairo/Egypt, the sale of a ṭallīt, and various other transactions. Dating: probably ca. 16th century. Fully preserved. Needs examination.
Possibly the address of a letter to [Ḥal]fon ha-Levi b. M[...] from [...] b. Yiṣḥaq Sijilmāsī.
Probably a letter concerning legal matters, or else a legal query. Mentions "our master" and "Gaʾon" and witnesses and oaths several times. The join is not certain.
Possibly a letter. The whole folio is preserved but the text is too faded to read.
Scorpion amulet

Informal note addressed to a mother. In Hebrew. Dating: ca. 15th–17th century. The sender says that a certain gentile is harassing him for money but 'the sage' (ha-ḥakham) didn't want to give the gentile any more than three ducats (peraḥim), and he doesn't know what to do. 

On verso there is a doodle of a stick figure.
Verso: Minute fragment of an Arabic document. Resembles the format of the Ikhshīdid fiscal documents but there is too little preserved to confirm. Reused for Hebrew literary text on recto.
Verso: Some sort of note in Arabic script, maybe an order of payment. Headed by the glyph. Recto is covered with later jottings in Hebrew script.

Bifolio containing accounts in Arabic script and Greek/Coptic numerals. There are also Hebrew jottings at 180 degrees, probably a secondary use. Many names mentioned, e.g. Abū ʿAlī Ibn Ḥaffāḍ(?); Aḥmad al-Ṣabbān; Abū Manṣūr; Abū l-Ḥajjāj; Futūḥ al-Shāmī. Also may mention bāb al-futūḥ.
Bifolio containing accounts in Hebrew script. Late. Mentions names such as al-ʿAbbāsī, Maymūn, Bū l-Khayr, and Naḥmas. There is also literary text at 180 degrees.
Verso: Small fragment of an Arabic document, likely state-related as recto was reused by a prolific scribe who reused many other state documents.
A long set of amulets for Abū l-Ḥasan ʿAlī b. Rayyisa, including that he will find favor in the eyes of Jaʿfar known as Sayf al-Dawla, who will only be able to speak well of him.

Legal record (#123) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 40v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 28 Sivan 5329 AM (1569 CE). Avraham the elder (ha-zaqen) b. Manṣūr al-Fūlādī acknowledges that he owes a debt of 20 ashrafi in the form of a charitable loan to ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Levi. MCD.

description: Verso: Reused fragment with two partial lines of an Arabic state document. Mentions a group of people who want help (وان غرضهم مساعدة). Reused for Hebrew literary text.
Verso: Fragment of an Arabic state document mentioning the dīwān. Reused on recto for a halakhic discussion or commentary.

Bifolio. Secondary use: Draft of formulaic phrases in Hebrew, Aramaic, Judaeo-Arabic, and a couple words in Arabic addressed to some dignitary (likely anonymous based on the פ for פלוני). According to FGP there is occult/magical text here, but that does not seem accurate.

Recto: Right half of a letter in Arabic addressed to a brother and/or son (perhaps a younger brother?). In Judaeo-Arabic. Dating: probably no earlier than ca. 15th century. Mentions weeping from loneliness; greetings for Yosef; Masʿūda; the sender's wife. The late colloquial word באש appears. Mentions something "in Arabic." Verso is also a shorter note in a similar handwriting that appears to have been written after the page was torn in half. Begins with a mention of R. Barukh, then Masʿūd of Istanbul, then the noble and enlightened sage Masʿūd b. Barukh. The next three lines are cryptic (something magical?) and conclude with ושלום and maybe the sender's rudimentary signature. Merits further examination.
Unidentified document in Arabic. Dated: Jumād[a] I 1219 AH (1804 CE). Requires further examination.
Document in Arabic. Late. Looks like accounting.
Late accounts in Arabic.
Accounts in Judaeo-Arabic and some Arabic. Mainly organized by parshiyot. Also mentioning some names such as Abū l-ʿAlāʾ.
State document in Arabic. Fragments of 4 lines are preserved.
Medical treatise in Hebrew. Late. Mentions diseases such as leprosy, gout, hemorrhoids, and an anecdote involving Ibn Rushd and the caliph and the theriac of Galen.
Two lines of accounts in Arabic and Coptic numerals: "I collected from Maḥāsin 3 nuqra dirhams less a kharrūba." The main text is a calendar in Hebrew script.
Verso may be a fragment of a letter in Arabic, possibly containing a word in Hebrew in the midst of the Arabic unless this is from a separate use. Needs examination.
Small fragment of a letter in Judaeo-Arabic: מנהם שי אם לא . . . מוצלה . . . הם מן כל . . . אלמ . . .
Small fragment of a letter in Judaeo-Arabic, containing a couple words from the opening greetings.
Possibly a letter in Judaeo-Arabic. Small fragment. Mentions חצרה מולאי אלחבר

Recto: Legal fragment in the hand of Ḥalfon b. Menashshe. Involving a debt and a certain Yefet, but unclear if any details are preserved. 

Verso contains rhymed Hebrew lines about redemption written in a different hand (ממלכה אשר בטלה עוד תשוב כתחלה ובת היתה בגולה פתאום תראה גאולה . . . ) . .

description: Table of Greek/Coptic numerals (accounting?).

Legal record (#124) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 40v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 11 Tammuz 5329 AM (1569 CE). Farjallah b. Yehuda al-Levi acknoledges a debt to ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Ḥakīm b. Rabbi Yehuda ha-Rofe ha-dayyan and commits to repay the sum of 10 ashrafī in two installments between the coming months of Elul and Ṭevet. The mention of ʿAbd al-Wāḥid's potential surname al-Ḥakīm points to the possibility that his father's titles are solely professional in nature "ha-rofe ha-dayyan" (the physician, the judge), although Rofe and Dayyan are each potential Karaite surnames. ʿAbd al-Wāḥid appears in another entry (#111) with the surname or individual nickname al-Ḥakīm but appears without it one page earlier in the court register (record #122). MCD.

description: Booklet of piyyuṭim in the hand of Moshe b. Levi ha-Levi. Many pages preserved.
Verso: Fragment of a state document in Arabic. Beautiful hand. Mentions الحاج . . . واحضر الحجة على . . .
Technical recipe in Arabic written on parchment, likely medical. Hebrew literary text on recto.
Ownership note on a page probably originally from a quire of piyyuṭ. "Purchased by Shelomo b. Nissim Beḥir ha-Parnasim."
Poem in Judaeo-Arabic dramatizing the events of the book of Esther. Join: Alan Elbaum.

Legal record (#125) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 41r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 14 Av 5329 AM (1569 CE). The scribal hand of this entry is not that of Avraham b. Yeshaʿyyahu Tūrīzī, who likely penned most of the court register. Marital dispute case in which Ṣedaqa b. ʿAbd al-Daʾīm testifies that "for five year's from [today's] date he has not resided with his wife Farj bt. Avraham al-Levi." The phrasing of the court record then becomes somewhat unclear: "...he has not resided with his wife Farj bt. Avraham al-Levi at his siblings' not masculine (pl.) nor feminine (pl.)" (ענד אכואתה לא דכורה ולא אלאנאת). These two adjectives are in the plural form and were probably included by the scribe to depict "siblings" as a group comprised of both brothers and sisters (as opposed to solely male or female siblings). It seems extraordinary that Ṣedaqa's estranged wife would be living with his siblings, but later on in the record he states that he will no longer accuse his wife with the words: "you separated me and my family" (lit. "you split/separated between me and my family"). The dispute ends with the stipulation: "and he (Ṣedaqa) has acquired a house and his desire is for his mother to reside with him, may there be peace." MCD.
scholarship_records: Matthew Dudley's digital edition (2026).

description: Literary: prayers. This unusual fragment from the Cairo Geniza contains an Aramaic version of the Hebrew prayer Ve-ilu finu (“Were Our Mouths [Filled with Song]”). This prayer is mentioned in the Babylonian Talmud (b. Berakhot 59b). During the geonic period it became a standard part of the closing of the morning psalms–daily in Palestinian communities and on Sabbath and festivals in Babylonian communities. A variety of versions of the prayer survive. This Aramaic version clearly sought to mimic the Hebrew one. A number of Aramaic piyyutim (liturgical poems) for Sabbaths and festivals were composed in Byzantium, suggesting a possible source for this text. This version may have been meant specifically for Passover. (Information from Posen Library)
