description: This Aramaic amulet, found in the Cairo Geniza, requests healing from disease and protection from the evil eye for a woman named Bunyana bint Yaman. The scribe who wrote this text seems to have written other amulets as well. This text invokes a number of angels and divine names and includes several biblical verses. As in many late antique and medieval magical texts, the formulas are recycled and appear in other magical literature. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Avi Steinhart, "Amulet against Disease and the Evil Eye," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: This Aramaic amulet, found in the Cairo Geniza, was composed for the protection of Ḥabibah bint Zuhra during childbirth. The amulet requests that the zodiacal sign Leo prevail over any forces that might endanger Ḥabibah during this dangerous time. Several powerful spirits, both good and evil, are identified in this text, which also invokes the biblical matriarchs Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah. Like many such texts, it includes magical letter combinations. A rather lengthy example, this amulet survives on two pieces of paper. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Avi Steinhart, "Amulet for Protection in Childbirth," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: Legal record (#126) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 41r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 14 Av 5329 AM (1569 CE), the same day as the preceding entry on f. 41r. The scribal hand of this entry is that of Avraham b. Yeshaʿyyahu Tūrīzī, who likely penned most of the court register, but the preceding record was penned by a different scribe. Conditional betrothal dissolution agreement between Reʾuven b. ʿAbd al-Bāqī al-Levi and ʿAbd al-Mejīt b. Aharon al-parnas al-Kohen, with the latter representing Reʾuven's unnamed fiancée. ʿAbd al-Mejīt is the betrothed woman's father. The conditional dissolution of the betrothal is based on Reʾuven's pending travel plans: if he leaves Cairo (or possibly Egypt) for longer than two months, then the khalāṣ document is to be delivered by his legal proxy Ibrahīm b. Yehuda ha-dayyan ha-rofe. Reʾuven's legal representative is likely the brother of the man in whose home this entry was recorded, ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Ḥakīm, whose full nomenclature appears in record #124 in the same court register (PGPID 42076). This page of the court register may have been detached due to damage and thus appears with the pagination folio 50 in the RNL microfilm. MCD.
scholarship_records: Matthew Dudley's digital edition (2026).

description: The Treatise on Abrogation of the Law (Kitāb naskh al-shar‘) is concerned with one of the most pressing questions of interreligious debate among Jews, Christians, and Muslims: the mutability of divine law. The doctrine of abrogation undergirded both Christian and Muslim claims about revelation, and Muslims analyzed it according to rigid linguistic features and particular theological claims. The Treatise on Abrogation of the Law survives in two versions. In this excerpt from the second version, Samuel ben Ḥofni Ga’on tackles some routine linguistic issues and relates some of the varied approaches taken by Jews to this doctrine. This work survived only in the Cairo Geniza but was quoted repeatedly in the later Middle Ages. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Dora Zsom, "Treatise on Abrogation of the Law," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: This silluk (a term for the last of a series of piyyutim written for the first three blessings of the Amidah), preserved in the Cairo Geniza, was to be recited on the Ninth of Av at the conclusion of a long series of piyyutim in the Amidah, before the conclusion of the blessing “. . . who consoles Zion and builds Jerusalem.” The text asks for revenge against Assyria, perhaps a stand-in for contemporary persecutors of the Jews. This silluk serves as a transition to the Kedushah, which begins with the words “Holy, holy, holy”–hence the word holy in the last line. The poem was once attributed to Eleazar be-Rabbi Qillir, although this credit is not generally accepted by scholars today. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Gabriel Wasserman, "Time to rebuke the beast of the forest," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: This penitential selihah survives in several manuscripts found in the Cairo Geniza. It is based on the conceit that the Jewish people is “sick”—that is, suffering in exile—and that God can heal this illness by bringing redemption. Aaron Ibn al-‘Ammānī (12th century) signed his given name twice in the acrostic of this poem. Each line in this rhythmic and compressed work has three internal rhymes, precisely sixteen syllables, and ends with the word holeh (ill). (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Gabriel Wasserman, "The pool (the pool!)," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: Piyyuṭ by Yaʿaqov bar Dunash bar ʿAqiva expanding on a poem by Elʿazar be-Rabbi Qillir contrasting God (“the lofty king”) with earthly rulers (“the wretched king”). Each stanza consists of five lines, each beginning with the same letter. The initial letters together form an acrostic spelling out the author's name. Each stanza closes with a biblical verse, a technique widespread by the tenth century. (Information from the Posen Library) The Posen Library entry for this poem says that it is for Rosh ha-Shana (the Jewish new year). That is true of the original poem by Elʿazar be-Rabbi Qillir, but recto, right and verso, left indicate that this bifolio was part of a Yom Kippur maḥzor: the recto contains the header "Qedushta for mussaf of Yom Kippur" and the verso contains part of the confessions recited on Yom Kippur. So it appears that Yaʿaqov bar Dunash bar ʿAqiva used Qillir's Rosh ha-Shana piyyut as an inspiration and basis for a new piyyut for Yom Kippur. (Information from Ariella Pressner)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Gabriel Wasserman, "The lofty king—He sits in His hidden place," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: This is an ahavah poem composed by Mevorakh ben Se‘adya (early 12th century), for recitation during the synagogue service inside the blessing “who blesses his people Israel with love [ahavah],” immediately preceding the Shema‘ in the morning service. Marked by the repetition of words, this strophic poem is written in a folk style popular among Jews and Arabs during this period. Here, drawing on Sufi traditions, the poet evokes the pool as the source of divine blessing from which blessing flows to the Jewish people. The “masters” of the pool here are the Jewish people. This poem has also been interpreted as having been meant to celebrate a wedding. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Gabriel Wasserman, "You are God, who does wonders," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: This Hebrew text presents a detailed account of a journey to the heavens, perhaps to guide future heaven-bound travels. Many of the themes in this text relate to Hekhalot literature in general and to the early text Measure of the Divine Body (Shi‘ur komah) in particular. The beginning of this manuscript is damaged, but it tells of an encounter between R. Ishmael and the angel Ozhayah, who is describing the features of the name Tandrael, associated with a powerful master or rabbi in Babylonia. The second part of this excerpt describes the sixth and seventh heavens (the translation uses the Hebrew word hekhal) and the dangers of the journeys there. No date has been established for this text, but it must have been written between the completion of the Talmud in the sixth century and the eleventh century, when the extant manuscript was copied. Unbracketed ellipses indicate lacunae in the text. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Michael D. Swartz, "Seal of the Chariot," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3. ; Michael D. Swartz, The Mechanics of Providence: The Workings of Ancient Jewish Magic and Mysticism (Mohr Siebeck, 2018).

description: This Byzantine Haggadah (10th-13th century) preserves uniquely Byzantine traditions and reflects some of the variability of the Haggadah in the medieval period. These excerpts derive from the end of the retelling of the Exodus story and the recitation of Psalms 113 and 114 (Hallel, which begins here with the words “We say before him” and ends with the words “a spring of water”) prior to the consumption of the festive meal. It is noteworthy that, like many rites, this text omits one of the blessings over the second cup of wine. The Judaeo-Greek instructions in this text are italicized. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Nicholas de Lange, "A Byzantine Haggadah," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3. ; Nicholas de Lange, Greek Jewish Texts from the Cairo Genizah (Mohr, 1996).

description: The Book of the Correction of the Negligence Found in the Books of the Head of the Academy, al-Fayyūmī (Kitāb istidrāk al-sahw al-mawjūd fī kutub ra’s al-mathība al-Fayyūmī), is a book by Mubashshir ben Nissi ha-Levi criticizing Se‘adya Ga’on—who was often referred to as the Fayyūmī, as he was born in the Fayyūm region of Egypt. It covers a number of philosophical, exegetical, and legal topics. Its intent remains unclear; some scholars have seen it as an attempt to undercut Se‘adya’s authority, while others believe that Mubashshir simply sought to avoid the naïve acceptance of authority known in Arabic as taqlīd. Recent scholarship has highlighted that Mubashshir was one of many Rabbanites in Baghdad who staunchly opposed Se‘adya’s leadership, siding with traditional Iraqi elites who clashed with the Egyptian-born gaon. This passage, from the introduction, proclaims that the author will show no loyalty to Se‘adya and instead will verify all religious matters for himself. (Information from Posen Library)

Stern, "The Beginning of Mubashshir’s Critique of Sa‘adya Gaon’s Writings," Revue des Études Juives 126 (n.p., 1967), 113–17. ; S. M. Stern, "The Book of the Correction of the Negligence Found in the Books of the Head of the Academy, al-Fayyūmī: Introduction," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: This version of the Grace after Meals, preserved in the Cairo Geniza in two fragments, has aspects that follow Palestinian traditions, aspects that follow Babylonian traditions, and certain phrases that belong to other rites entirely. In the manuscript, the scribe recorded a longer and shorter version of the Grace after Meals, with the suggestion that the shorter text, presented here, be recited on weekdays. The text of the prayer and the initial instructions are entirely in Hebrew. (Information from Posen Library)

Reif, "Grace after Meals for Weekdays according to Cairo Geniza Fragments," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3. ; Stefan C. Reif, Jewish Prayer Texts from the Cairo Genizah (Brill, 2016).

description: This poetic rendition of the Amidah survived in the Cairo Geniza on folios that were written by three different scribes of varying caliber; perhaps one page was lost, or they were copied by a teacher and a student. It appears likely that the text is Palestinian in origin and has its roots in centuries-old forms that were popular in that community. It follows the skeletal outline of the Amidah that was shared by Rabbanite Jews, and it testifies to the instability of the Jewish liturgy in the medieval period. It is followed by a text for Purim (also included here), which may mean that it was part of an originally larger liturgical collection. Unbracketed ellipses indicate lacunae in the manuscript. (Information from Posen Library; NB translation only covers pages 1–4)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Stefan C. Reif, "Poetic Version of the Amidah," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3. ; Stefan C. Reif, Jewish Prayer Texts from the Cairo Genizah (Brill, 2016).

description: This Passover Haggadah text, preserved in the Cairo Geniza and written on parchment, presents a striking medieval version of the Passover ritual. This version of the Mah nishtanah (Four Questions; lit., “How is [this night] different”), which has ancient roots (see m. Pesaḥim 10), reflects different practices from those usual today. Among the hundreds of copies of texts for the seder, this text stands out for its calligraphic hand. The instructions are in Judeo-Arabic, the prayers are in Hebrew, and the midrash is in Aramaic. Italicized words, apart from the Hebrew biblical verses, are in Judeo-Arabic. The last paragraph is in Aramaic. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Stefan C. Reif, "How Is This Night Different? (Mah nishtanah)," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3. ; Stefan C. Reif, Jewish Prayer Texts from the Cairo Genizah (Brill, 2016).

description: The Book of Musta‘īnī (Kitāb Musta‘īnī, ca. 1106) by Yūsuf Ibn Biklārish al-Isrā’īlī consists of a mostly alphabetical list of 704 medicinal components, identified in Arabic and presented in tabular format. The author names the ingredients in a startling variety of languages, including Berber, Greek, Latin, Persian, the Spanish vernacular, and Syriac, although not in a systematic way. This Judeo-Arabic fragment survived in the Cairo Geniza. (The Kitāb Musta‘īnī also survives in several Arabic manuscripts, as the work remained useful for centuries.) Although the author originally included five columns in his table, this copyist reduced it to three. The text is presented here in paragraphs instead of columns. The first line gives the name of the substance (here in italics) and its qualities; the second paragraph provides its synonyms and then its benefits; the third, if there is one, gives an acceptable substitute for it. Unbracketed ellipses indicate lacunae in the manuscript. (Information from Posen Library)
scholarship_records: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3: Encountering Christianity and Islam. ; Yaron Serri and Efraim Lev, "A Judaeo-Arabic Fragment of Ibn-Biklarish’s Kitab al-Musta‘īnī, Part of a Unique 12th-Century Tabular Medical Book Found in the Cairo Genizah (T-S Ar.44.218)," Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 20, no. 4 (n.p., 2010), 407–40. ; Yaron Serri and Efraim Lev, "The Book of Musta‘īnī," in Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization (Yale University Press, 2026), vol. 3.

description: Legal record (#127) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 41v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 2 Elul [5329 AM] (1569 CE), with the scribe implying that the year is the same as the preceding entry (סנה תאר׳). Brief and possibly incomplete record reporting that Hārūn b. Shemuʾel al-Fūlādī married Khaṣṣ bt. ʿAbd al-Jaffār al-Fūlādī. The bride is listed as a minor (קאצר/قاصر). The witnesses to the marriage are Shelomo ha-Rofe and Yosef b. ʿAbd al-Daʾīm al-Levi al-Qudsī. The subsequent entry (#128) on the same page lays out conditions for the couple's marriage. MCD.
scholarship_records: Matthew Dudley's digital edition (2026).

description: Legal record (#128) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 41v of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 2 Elul 5329 AM (1569 CE), the same day as the previous entry which constitutes a brief record of the marriage between Khaṣṣ bt. ʿAbd al-Jaffār al-Fūlādī, a minor, and the groom Hārūn b. Shemuʾel al-Fūlādī. This subsequent record consists of the conditions for the couple's marriage: the groom will not wed a second wife for at least ten years and there are limits on his travel and residency outside his father's house for the same timespan. This condition is rare enough that it points to the possibility the groom was also a minor but not listed as such. For the bride's legal status as a minor (קאצר), see the previous entry in the court register. Travel-related stipulations are normally laid out according to spousal consent in early modern Karaite marital documents. MCD.
scholarship_records: Matthew Dudley's digital edition (2026).

description: Piyyuṭ in the hand of Moshe b. Levi ha-Levi.
Ownership or dedication note (bi-rasm...) for Yosef b. Shela.

Fol. 2v, right page, 90 degrees: Fiscal document. Confirming the disbursement of funds related to the "lofty rescripts" in a certain year (504 AH?): واطلق بالتوقيعات العالية في شهور . . . . Some sort of ʿalāma or registration at upper left.
Ownership note for Hillel b. Meyuppe.
Ownership note for Yosef b. Araḥ.

Fol. 1: Jotted accounts in Judaeo-Arabic. Late? Mentions fulūs. There are also jottings in other hands including poetic blessings in Hebrew for the new Nagid and the opening of a letter, and writing exercises.

Verso: Jottings in Judaeo-Arabic about people fighting and/or playing. "Abū l-Munā and Barakāt were quarreling. . . Abū l-Faraj the dyer of red was playing and fighting. . . Abū l-ʿAlāʾ was playing. . . Abū l-Faraj and his brother Ibn al-Ṣabbāgh were playing, and I said to them, "I'm going to go write your names(?)." They said, "By God, we don't care [. . . .]." The name Abū l-Munā also appears in Arabic at the top. The verb qaʿada appears in each of these entries as an auxiliary verb (rather than literal "sitting"). 

Recto has a catena of biblical verses (information in part from CUDL.)

Recto is a long piyyuṭ. 

Verso contains an extremely faded text block in Judaeo-Arabic, possibly documentary. At 180 degrees to this there are some names, including the phrase "from Ṣāliḥ b. Yosef b. Khalfa al-Maghribī"; the line underneath has the name of one of his brothers (" . . b. Yosef al-Maghribī b. Khalfa"); the line underneath that begins "May God in His mercy. . ." (אללה ברחמתה. . .). There was a well-known Maghribī merchant Yosef b. Khalfa active in the mid-11th century. This might be the address of a letter based on the "from" before Sāliḥ's name.
Verso: Dedication and ownership notes. "Saʿadya b. Aharon wrote this for Yosef b. Berakha. . ."; "Refuʿa ha-Levi b. [...] purchased. . ."
Colophon with the date 1501 Seleucid = 1189/90 CE and the name Yefet b. Yosef ha-Levi in a box.
Verso - Ownership note: "this is what Yaḥyā b. Ḥalfon had copied for him. . ."

Verso: Poetic letter in Hebrew wih slightly widened line spacing addressed to a dignitary. Consisting entirely of praises and blessings. The addressee is referred to as Nasi and Nagid in the last two lines. Either the continuation is missing, or this is only a draft of the opening section. 

Recto contains piyyuṭ in a different hand.

Bifolio containing piyyuṭ and scribal practice. One of the pages contains a brief petition-like note addressed to a woman (al-sitt al-jalīla) with a taqbīl and a request to send the writer a codex of Jeremiah: עבד חצרה אלסת אלגלילה אטאל אללה בקאהא ואדאם עזהא ונעמאהא וכבת חסדתהא ואעדאהא יקבל אלארץ בין ידי חצרתהא ויסל תפצלהא אן תוגהי לעבדך מצחף ירמיה.

On this genre, see Oded Zinger, "Gender and the Art of Asking," Medieval Globe 9, no. 2 (2023): 103–27.

Account in Arabic script, probably fiscal based on the hand and the extravagant line spacing. The top line mentions al-jarīda al-madkhūra. L. 6 refers to a waẓīfa. Mentions quantities in arṭāl. Reused for Hebrew piyyuṭ on recto. Needs further examination.
Probably a draft of a panegyric for a dignitary. On verso at 180 degrees refers to a Nagid. The hand resembles that of Avraham Ibn Yijū - needs examination.

Verso: Medical prescription in Arabic. 

On recto there is Hebrew piyyuṭ.
Recto contains piyyuṭ. Verso contains instructions in Judaeo-Arabic for certain prayers to be said in the synagogue. May mention jinn in the bottom line.

Fragment from the bottom of a legal document written on parchment. Dated Ṣafar 261 AH = November/December 874 CE. This is therefore the oldest Arabic document in the Geniza and likely the oldest dated document in any language in the Geniza. Most of what is preserved consists of people's names. From l. 8 onward (and possibly beginning earlier in this fragment), all of the names are followed by the witness formula وكتب شهادته, in some cases written as a ligature (وكتبـشهادته). Requires further study. 

On the other oldest dated documents of the Geniza, see Eve Krakowski and Sacha Stern, “The ‘Oldest Dated Document of the Cairo Genizah’ (Halper 331)," Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 31.3 (2021): 617–634.

Reused on verso for Hebrew piyyuṭ for Shemini ʿAṣeret.

Identified by Alan Elbaum in August 2026.

Ownership/dedication notes: "written for Elʿazar b. ʿOvadya." A version of this appears also in Arabic: "this is for Abū Manṣūr b. ʿAbdallāh al-Isrāʾīlī" followed by blessings, concluding with a mention of someone or something al-Iskandarāniyya. The left page contains additional names including Ḥasan [ha-Ko]hen b. Ḥalfon and Yosef b. Ḥalfon ha-Kohen, then Elʿazar and Ṣedaqa b. Yosef and Yosef.
Literary work describing the liturgy in the hand of Yedutun ha-Levi.
Colophon for מסכת דרך ארץ זעירא. Written for himself by Berakhot ha-Levi ha-Mumḥe Ner ha-Ḥazzanim b. Yosef ha-Ḥazzan on Wednesday, 1 Elul 1487 Seleucid = 8 August 1176 CE, in Damīra.
Verso: Order of payment in Arabic, headed by the glyph. For 450 of something. Needs examination.

The main text is Talmudic. The margins are entirely filled with a technical text in a mixture of Judaeo-Arabic and Arabic regarding calculations about hours of the day. Mentions the term taḥwīl frequently. There are more joins listed on FGP.

Narrow vertical strip of a text in Judaeo-Arabic, probably a business letter (ביע . . . כאן לא . . . תמן להא . . דת אן אל . . . אלסמ[ס?]רה . . . [ינ?]עם מולי . .). Some of the letter shapes resemble those of Maimonides but the handwriting is not his.

Copy of masekhet ʿeruvin. Fol. 2r contains several ownership notes, including for its scribe (musaṭṭiruhā) Elʿazar b. Saʿadya b. Yosef; then Nadiv al-[...] b. Yosef; then Shelomo b. Avraham known as Dhahabī; then Shelomo b. Yeshuʿa b. Shelomo ha-Kohen. There is another illegible note at upper left.

Verso: Last line of a legal document in Hebrew dated according to the creation. None of the other details are preserved. It's unclear if this was originally part of a larger document . Recto contains Talmudic text.

Bifolio. The main text is a very detailed list of the forbidden sexual relations (ʿarayot). In the margin at the bottom of recto, there is an informal note addressed to Mūsā requesting him to "come speak with me in the house, quickly, quickly" (אלשיך אלאגל מוסי ינעם יכלמני פי אלבית סרעה סרעה ושלום). The margins on verso contain various jottings in Arabic and Greek/Coptic numerals.

Verso: Colophon with an embellished signature by the scribe Yehosef b. Ṣedaqa. Written on Monday, 1 Elul. There are writing exercises in Arabic in a chancery hand reading "thiqat al-mulk dhū l-riʾāsa ṣanīʿat amīr al-muʾminīn" and a similar phrase on the facing page. The facing page also includes an unfinished note in Judaeo-Arabic: "I learned that the bearer of this note is a Muslim man who knows that the lofty presence. . . " (אתצל בי אן מוצל הדה אלרקעה רגל מסלם יערף באן חצרתה אלסאמיה)
Fol. 3v: Brief jotted accounts in Judaeo-Arabic mentioning Nāṣirī silver. There is also an ownership note for Moshe b. Hillel the descendant of [...]. This page is part of a larger quire.
Mainly literary. At the bottom of verso there is a list of names: Avraham, Yaʿaqov, Netanʾel, ʿAmram, Ḥalfon, Yefet ha-...]; Ṭahor, Elʿazar, Moshe, Ṭahor. Dating: probably 12th or 13th century.
The main text is literary/halakhic. On verso at 90 degrees there are accounts in Arabic and Greek/Coptic numerals. Mentions Bū l-ʿAlāʾ, Yūsuf, Abū l-Ḥasan, and someone's brother.

Official correspondence in Arabic. Wide line spacing. 

Four lines preserved: . . ذلك ولما حضروا واعادوا . . . قررنا الامر على ما كاتبناك به من ان يكون كل منهم يصلي في البيعة من غير ان يستبدها(؟) واحد دون اخر وان يدخلوا الى الحضرة . . . الشيخ ابي نصر داود بن اسحق . . . الشيخ ابي سعد . . . 

The sender is reporting on a decision that was taken after a group of people arrived: that each of them will "pray in the homage" (yuṣallī fī l-bayʿa) without any one of them oppressing or perhaps imposing their version on the other (min ghayr an yastabidduhā(?) wāḥid dūn ākhar). The meaning of this unclear but presumably has to do with a controversy over whose authority should be recognized in prayers. Then mentions Abū Naṣr Dāwūd b. Isḥāq (this is probably the Qaraite courtier Abū Naṣr David b. Yiṣhaq ha-Levi active in the first half of the 11th century) and Abū Saʿd (al-Tustarī?).

There are several unrelated fragments sharing this shelfmark, of which the only documentary one is fol. 5. 

Fol. 5v: Legal document written by Mevorakh b. Natan. Dated: Tammuz 1481 Seleucid = June/July 1170 CE. Directly related to the document on recto. Contains many convoluted details regarding rent of the aforementioned house; Wahb the blind cantor (אלחזן אלצריר); and perhaps a dispute between Maḥfūẓ the beadle of the synagogue and al-Rayyis Abū Zikrī regarding who collected what sum for what month. The document states that Mevorakh b. Natan he-Ḥaver and the parnas Abū l-Faḍl testified that al-Rayyis Abū Zikrī received 140 dirhams from Karīm al-Ṭabbākh out of the rent of Dār Mahra, of which 2/3 belongs to the qodesh (אלתי אלתלתי מנהא ללמקאדסה). Also mentions testimony of Abū Sahl b. al-Ahuv (a.k.a. Abū Sahl Levi b. Levi), and something to do with the house of Sitt Kitmān located in Sūq Barbar, and later to someone who "ceased holding the headship in Sivan of [...]" (פי הדה אלריאסה אלתי אנצרף מנהא פי סיון). This might suggest that al-Rayyis Abū Zikrī is none other than Sar Shalom ha-Levi, though the timeline doesn't quite fit, as he rose to the position of Head of the Jews in 1170 and is believed to have lost it to Maimonides only in 1171. The document is signed by Yaʿaqov b. Yosef ha-Kohen, Shemuel b. Saʿadya ha-Levi, and Aharon b. Yaʿ[aqov ha-Levi] ha-Melammed.

description: This prayer (al ha-nisim), added to the Amidah and Grace after Meals during Hanukkah, and to other Hanukkah texts, is preserved on a twelfth-century bifolium in the Cairo Geniza. The first part presents passages from Targum Onkelos on Numbers 7, a part of the Torah read during Hanukkah. This version of Al ha-nisim combines both Egyptian and Eastern traditions. The text closes with instructions in Judaeo-Arabic. The copyist of this manuscript was not particularly skilled and had to correct several areas. It has been suggested that this text was for personal use. (Information from Posen Library)

description: These three blessings, all preserved in the Cairo Geniza, were likely recited in Rabbanite synagogues in Fustāt (Old Cairo) or its surroundings. The first is a blessing recited prior to the recitation of the second chapter of m. Shabbat (which begins “With what may one kindle?”) on Sabbath eve. The practice of reciting this chapter in synagogue may have anti-Karaite roots, as Rabbanites sought to validate their custom of kindling lights that would burn on the Sabbath, whereas Karaites rejected the use of any fire on the Sabbath. The second blessing was to be said for readings from the Writings (Ketuvim) on the Sabbath, and the third for Psalms. [these prayers are also preserved in T-S Or.1080 3.52 and T-S NS 155.1] (Information from Posen Library)

Bifolio containing a very lengthy and detailed Hebrew narrative of business dealings, possibly intended as a draft or copy of a letter, or possibly related to a legal document or legal query. Dating: ca. 16th century based on the mention of the currency sharīfī, al-Khwājā ʿUthmān, and Turkish-influenced terms (e.g. ועשיתי עמו בזאר means "I made a business deal with him," likely a calque from the Turkish "pazar etmek"). The writer is located in Fustat/Cairo (פה מצרים) and also mentions places including Bulaq and Alexandria. The story begins with a purchase of a large batch of galangal (khawlanjān), which turned out to be partly rotten and worm-eaten, from a Muslim man and from a probably Jewish man known as שניי (Shanyī? a variant of Shanjī?). The writer tried to sieve out the rotten parts as best he could and he then struck a deal with a Christian to sell it to him. As they were waiting for the official weigher (qabbānī, shoqel) to arrive, Shanyī arrived and impounded the galangal. The writer tried to find Shanyī to ask why he did this, but he could find only his own brother-in-law (apparently closly associated with Shanyī) who explained that "the galangal you purchased is worthless" and that he had it impounded to prevent the writer from making a bad deal with the Christian over it. Time passed, and the Christian continued to harass the writer for the galangal that he had purchased but which the writer was unable to turn over to him. He considered suing Shanyī but refrained both because he did not want the Christian to hear about this matter, and because "I know his cruel heart with me, and he would simply throw it in the river/sea and not return it to me." The writer acknowledges that he does owe 14 sharīfīs to Shanyī (which may explain Shanyī's behavior toward him). The brokers (סרסורים) intervened and suggested that half of the deal be canceled and half continued. Eventually, the writer intended to travel on a Friday and summoned the Rayyis (ship's captain?) to pack his goods, but Shanyī came and held back the ship due to the oustanding 14 sharīfīs. The writer describes "almost going mad" and his "great fear" over this. He then produced a bag of opium weighing 27.5 raṭls, intending to leave it as collateral, with the aid of his brother-in-law Yosef. He then traveled onward to Bulaq. Months later, Shemuʾel al-ʿAjam arrived in Alexandria requesting his opium. Therefore the writer sent the 14 sharīfīs to Shanyī, intended for the brother-in-law, but he refused to return the opium because he says "he still owes me 6 sharīfīs from another debt, give me 2, and I'll give you the opium." Later it appears that the 6 peraḥim (apparently the same as the 6 sharīfīs) were a debt owed by the late Yaʿaqov [...]. The writer remains extremely upset about the situation. He mentions al-Khwājā ʿUthmān, and the story cuts off around here.

Part of a copy of a poem by the wife of Dunash Ibn Labrāṭ, followed by the first part of a second poem, a reply from Ibn Labrāṭ to his wife. Ibn Labrāṭ (920-990 CE) was a Spanish poet, grammarian and commentator who worked in the service of Ḥasday Ibn Shapruṭ, the leader of the Jewish community in Spain. Ibn Labrāṭ had a contentious relationship with his contemporaries, but very little is known about his wife. Her poem—the only known medieval Hebrew poem by a woman —has been praised for its quality and poignancy: Will her love remember his graceful doe / her only son in her arms as he parted? / On her left hand he placed a ring from his right, / on his wrist she placed her bracelet. / As a keepsake she took his mantle from him, / and he in turn took hers from her. / Would he settle, now, in the land of Spain, / if its prince gave him half his kingdom? [translated by Peter Cole]. The couple appear to have separated reluctantly under difficult circumstances, resentfully described in another poem identified as being by Ibn Labrāṭ to his employer: I served you in sorrow, for all your wares are loathsome. / I will glean no grapes, nor will I gather corn. / I betrayed a young wife and sent her a writ of divorce. / I left my home, and abandoned the son that she bore. (T-S J2.71, f. 2v). Part of a copy of Ibn Labrāṭ’s response to his wife’s poem is preserved at T-S NS 143.46 (PGPID 39008): Were you seeking the day of my death when you wrote: / ‘Have you betrayed and abandoned your vows?’ / Could I betray a woman so wise / given by god as the bride of my youth? / Had my heart ever thought to leave you / I would have torn it into pieces. / For those who betray their beloved companion, / God brings down with the trials of foes. / Lions soon will devour his flesh, / and vultures will consume his blood. / Who resembles the stars of dawn […] [translated by Peter Cole]. (Information from CUDL)

This prayer, preserved in the Cairo Geniza, was included in a guide for Jewish pilgrims to the holy city of Jerusalem. The brief prayers in this guide, primarily consisting of biblical citations, were to be said as the pilgrim approached the city. The instructions in this text are in Judeo-Arabic and the prayers themselves in Hebrew. At least ten similar texts survive in the Cairo Geniza, showing their popularity. Specific verses are indicated for recitation at each of the city’s gates, sometimes borrowed from other liturgical passages. Information from the Posen Foundation.

description: Petition filed by a woman asking the help of the community since her husband did not return from his travels. In Judaeo-Arabic. In the hand of Ḥalfon b. Menashshe ha-Levi (fl. 1100–1138 CE). See also T-S NS J401m (PGPID 26466) regarding the same matter. Date not preserved. The woman brought her case before the court asking for an allowance in order to provide herself with living expenses. Her arguments were as follows: her husband left her for a short time and did not intend to spend the winter away from home; however, by that time he had already been absent more than six months. In order to support herself, she had had to sell whatever remained of her dowry. Even when he is present, he is abusive. Her request of the court was two-fold: a. as mentioned above, to fix her an allowance for living expenses, and b. to confirm in a recorded document that all that she was obliged to sell in order to survive should be regarded as due her from her husband. This latter request was immediately met; but a decision on the former request was delayed, with the hope that the husband would soon return. Because the husband delayed his return, and she repeated her requests for help, it was decided to grant the woman an allowance on a temporary basis. It seems that she was one of the notables of the city and she was not even deprived of her servants who were also taken into account when the amount of the allowance was determined. No signatures are extant. (Information from Gershon Weiss.)

description: Legal record (#135) in a court register/pinqas from a Karaite beit din in Cairo (on f. 44r of Yevr.-Arab. I 328). Dated: 20 Ḥeshvan 5329 AM (1568 CE). Marital dispute resolution agreement in which Raḍī b. Shemuʾel Berakha agrees to no longer strike nor curse his wife Ṭurfa bt. Shelomo Fayrūz, and to a wide variety of other conditions, such as: he will pay her the full delayed dowry mentioned in her ketubba if they end up getting divorced, and he agrees not to wed a second wife for at least 12 years (probably an extension from the couple's ketubba). There are also some conditions regarding where Ṭurfa is to reside as part of the resolution. Two aspects of this record are uncommon compared to the broader legal sub-genre of early modern Karaite documents that deal with marital disputes. Firstly, the husband agrees to pay a fine toward supporting the poor in the community if he violates these terms (normally this fine is payable to his wife or as a communal donation of olive oil to the synagogue). Secondly, Raḍī himself signs below the record as a legal party, which is rare within the court register Yevr.-Arab. I 328. MCD

There is also a crown pictured below "Москва" and variety of other items appear in the foreground. The print references the "brothers Aleksandar and Aleksii Makarović," which is repeated in Arabic script– probably Persian given that "برادر" is the translation for "brother." The section in Russian uses the hard sign Ъ and follows spelling conventions prior the 1917/1918 orthography reforms. Requires further examination. (MCD with information from Sasha Batz Stern)

Legal query addressed to Moshe Maimonides with his autograph responsum, signed Moshe. 

The query is about a debt between brothers; whether it is permissible for one of them to appoint an agent to sue his brother to repay the debt; and whether it makes s difference if they live in the same town or in different towns? 

Maimonides responds that it is reprehensible to appoint an agent with a power of attorney (based on the use of Ezekiel 18:18 in Shevuʿot 31a) unless there is a practical reason why the two cannot appear in court themselves (e.g., if they live in different towns or if one of them is sick).

Mentions: something "the great" (ha-gedola); Saturday; the eighth; someone prevented from presenting himself; witnesses; someone who should take with him what he is obliged to pay/weigh; Torah scrolls; Thursday; a garment; some people excusing themselves by saying they didn't hear the ban of excommunication, others with other excuses.

Concerning a man who is seeking repayment of a debt from another based on a 14-year-old contract, but he has lost the contract and he wants the defendant to take an oath. Should the plaintiff also be obligated to take an oath that he lost the contract? 

There are a few words in Arabic on verso, probably unrelated.

Legal query with responsum. Concerning a prominent synagogue which adjoins a bet midrash with an upper floor for scholars and guests. A gentile wished to buy the bet midrash and the upper floor but the city and communal leaders would not sell it to him. A few months later, one of the local (Jewish) judges handed over the building to the gentile in exchange for another plot of land for himself, and he began to take timber from the bet midrash and build on that land. 

The responsum states that the judge must endeavor to buy back the bet midrash from the gentile.

On verso there are a few words in Arabic: al-mamlūk al-malikī(?) . . . .

(Information mainly from Shmuel Glick via FGP.)

If the entry was originally dated, this section is lost to damage across the upper portion of the page. Nearby entries are dated c. 1568 CE. The subject matter of this record shifts from a standard debt acknowledgement and proxy appointment for debt collection at the opening of the text, to the issue of Farjallah lying about compensating Ṣedaqa Kohen.
